#4571. Christian Horner Doesn’t Sound Like He’s Done With Formula 1 Yet

“I feel like I’m too young to retire,” he says.

“How would you introduce yourself to somebody that doesn’t know you?” I ask the man across the table.

“Christian Horner,” he says, then without pause, “somebody that used to be involved in Formula 1.”

Considering this is a man who could have truthfully responded “Commander of the Order of the British Empire” or “husband of Ginger Spice,” the choice to define himself by his past rather than present or future is hard to miss. His is a familiar name and a familiar face to even casual F1 fans. The Brit’s sharp tongue and vaguely Daniel Craig-ish visage made him a lead character of Netflix’s Drive to Survive in its first years when his Red Bull Formula 1 team was banking win after win, thanks also to the talents of people like Max Verstappen and Adrian Newey.

But no hot streak lasts forever, no matter how good you (or the people you work with) are. Horner was ejected from the team after the 2025 British Grand Prix in the wake of both a sexual harassment accusation scandal the year before and a general downturn in the team’s performance, reportedly receiving a €60 million platinum parachute in exchange for his departure from the sport.

For most, that might seem a sign from the universe to take up a hobby—say, gentleman farmer. But Horner isn’t most men. He’s still out there, orbiting F1 like a geosynchronous satellite: a long ways off but still locked above it, looking down at the whole of the world he left. As such, he’s been speaking at industry events like Sportico Invest London and the Autosport Business Exchange in New York, where I sat down with him before he went on stage.

Unsurprisingly to anyone who saw him on Drive to Survive, or at any of the 10,000 media events he did during his F1 career, Horner still has plenty to say. Even if he is trying to be polite about it.

“The racing has been entertaining, don’t get me wrong. I’m watching these races and seeing cars overtaking in Melbourne and other circuits that you don’t normally overtake at,” he says when discussing the current F1 season. “But they’re not really overtakes as opposed to ... drive-pasts.”

He is not, it seems, a particular fan of the 2026 power unit regulations that have caused consternation amongst teams and fans alike by forcing the gas-electric hybrid propulsion systems to split their output 50/50 between internal combustion-sourced and electron-derived power. Horner describes it as the biggest issue for F1 to tackle at the moment. “You would assume it would be a relatively easy fix, just to change that ratio, but it seems a little more complicated,” he says. “You hear the drivers not liking how these cars are to drive, because you’re not rewarded for driving quickly through a fast corner, for example.”

“I think they’re doing the right thing for 2030,” he adds, referring to FIA president Mohammed Ben ‌Sulayem’s plans to ditch the current hybrid V-6 powertrains for V-8 units. “I think it’s unfortunate for the current presidency because he inherited this set of regulations. So of course, he’s looking to address that for the next round of significant change to engine spec.”

The 2026 season’s power unit frustrations haven’t been all bad, at least in terms of entertainment value. They’ve played a role in keeping the constructors’ championship battle interesting, even if the driver’s championship was swept away by wunderkind Kimi Antonelli.

“It’s interesting, I think different teams have had different moments this year,” he says. “Mercedes started very strong; Ferrari then had a moment where they looked like they were gonna put a challenge together around Barcelona time—seeing Lewis [Hamilton] win his first race, Charles [Leclerc] winning at Silverstone. And McLaren started to get their act together, looked pretty racy around Zanvoort and Budapest time, and then obviously, the Red Bull cars have come on strong.”

But those cars at front of the field are practically in a different league from the other seven teams in this season, which Horner—despite his own successes captaining Red Bull teams that ran the table with Brady-Belichick efficiency—says isn’t ideal for the sport. “I think you want as many cars in the fight as you can get, and the best way to achieve that is stability. Because then they all [close on] the same solutions, and just iterate those same solutions. So if you want close racing, just leave those regulations, those chassis regulations, alone. And you’ll see them all converge onto one solution—the better solution.”

In other words, simplify, then add budget. Formula 1, as he points out, is both one of the most expensive sports in the world and the biggest team sport on the planet. “You’ve got over 2000 team members between engine and chassis, all producing two cars for twenty-four races a year.” Running all as team principal, unsurprisingly, is like spinning plates and juggling bowling pins at the same time, even before factoring in the spotlight.

“Challenges ... there are many. There’s the scrutiny you come under. The politics, the competition of people trying to nick your staff, your drivers, your sponsors. It’s such a competitive industry. There’s so much at stake with large amounts of money involved” he says. “It’s dog-eat-dog in that respect. You gotta get up pretty early in the morning to stay ahead of the rest.”

Having done so for so many years—and most of those seeing an above-average amount of success for the position—certainly suggests the 52-year-old Brit has what Liam Neeson might describe as a particular set of skills. Would you, I ask him, eventually like to circle back to Formula 1?

“I think ...” Here, he pauses. “You know, I had an incredible run. I’m very proud of what I did. It didn’t end the way in the way I would have liked. I’m still relatively young ... I would only go back—knowing the sacrifices it takes—for the right project. Only if I was in a position where I could influence change, drive change within the organization, with like-minded people that wanted to win ... I’ve won close to one-third of the races I entered. I don’t want to go back just to take part.”

But he’s not pigeonholing himself. “I have time on my side to be able to make decisions. I feel like I’m too young to retire,” he says. “Honestly, sitting right here, right now, I have no idea where the next twelve months are going to take me. And I find that kind of exciting.”

Will Sabel Courtney is a contributing editor at Road & Track. A 12-year veteran of journalism, he formerly worked at Gear Patrol, The Drive, and RIDES Magazine, and contributed to the New York Daily News and Jalopnik, among other outlets. You can often find him test-driving new cars in New York City, cursing the slow-moving traffic surrounding him.

It takes a second or two for the turbocharger to spool up and push the Envista ahead in earnest, which feels to the driver like the engine is taking a slow, deep breath before moving ahead with any urgency. But the Envista's vibe isn't about speed or sporty driving. Instead, it's built for loping along comfortably and quietly. #4568. Bald eagle Shadow defends Kaydee and his nest from intruder

Published Nov 9, 2026 12:54 PM EST

Word to the wise: don’t mess with Shadow’s nest. For the first time in two weeks, the internet-famous bald eagle’s (Haliaeetus leucocephalus) vocals were heard on the camera that captures a 24/7 livestream of his nest in Southern California. Shadow’s potentially new partner Kaydee was also heard nearby and she landed on the nest.

However, just after landing, Kaydee was on high alert because another eagle was eyeing the nest from above. Shadow quickly responded with loud vocals, and came swooping past the nest. While the intruding eagle briefly followed Shadow away, it made a turn back towards the nest. Kaydee made more calls to Shadow and quickly flew out of the nest, as the intruder tried to land on the branches above her. Shadow returned to the nest, and put himself between Kaydee and the intruder above, and all three birds flew away. Eventually, Shadow perched on a nearby tree and was heard giving a warning call in a loud voice while standing watch. The scene that appeared straight out of a movie was another exciting moment for the eagles of Big Bear Valley.

“The brief encounter last night definitely showed Shadow and Kaydee defending the nest, protecting it and each other,” writes Friends of Big Bear Valley (FOBBV), the non-profit organization that runs the livestream. “What a delight to see them as they have truly been missed these past two weeks!”

According to FOBBV, Shadow is ALSO an “experienced master builder and knows exactly when it’s time to begin tidying up the nest, moving stick furniture or placing new guardrails or a baby gate.”

We still do not know if Shadow and Kaydee will mate this season. Bald eagle nesting officially begins in September, and lasts over six months, depending on when the the chicks fledge. Eggs are typically laid in January.  Viewers can follow Shadow and Kaydee and their journey on the nest via a 24/7 livestream.

Kaydee, formerly known as KD1, is a banded female bald eagle that has been spotted in Big Bear Valley following the death of Shadow’s former partner, Jackie. She was born in 2022, about 70 miles away from Big Bear Lake in the Prado Basin between Anaheim and Riverside, California. Coincidentally, her parents are also named Lucky and Ricky like Jackie’s parents, but they are a different eagle pair.

Kaydee was banded as part of the Orange County Water District’s work to track the eagles born in the area. These bands help biologists track and monitor the birds over time. Kaydee currently has a black spot on her head, but it may not be permanent. It’s possible that not all of her white feathers have come in or it could be tree sap or dirt. She also has two small bands on her legs. One is a small metal band, while the other is a lavender band with “KD1” on it.

Kaydee is almost five years old, so she is just about ready to mate. She was recently spotted on FOBBV’s livestream inspecting the nest and has also been seen hanging out near Shadow. Flying around Big Bear is completely normal behavior for young adult eagles at this time of year.

In January, Jackie laid two eggs in the nest, but ravens destroyed them. She later laid two more eggs that hatched in April and named Luna and Sandy. The name Sandy is in honor of FOBBV’s former executive director Sandy Steers who died from cancer in February.

On July 17, Jackie was found injured on the ground near Dana Point Park, California. Cell phone video from a witness confirmed that she had an altercation with two other subadult eagles. She successfully fended off the other eagles by turning over and using her talons, but could not fly far away.

She was transferred to the Ojai Raptor Center for care, where she was diagnosed with severe anemia. Her anemia worsened during the first week of August, the Ojai Raptor Center said that she was in unstable condition on August 9. Her packed cell volume (PCV) fell below percent, before rising to nine percent. Jackie died early in the morning on August 10. The necropsy did not reveal a single cause of death, and instead pointed to several factors including severe anemia, bird flu, blood clots in her wing and one kidney, and liver and lung abnormalities.

A memorial service was held on September 5 in Fawnskin, California, along with a second celebration of life called Wings Over Big Bear on October 3. The event featured representatives from FOBBV, the Yuhaaviatam of San Manuel Nation, and more.

#4567. Losing even one hour of sleep can make you more susceptible to scams

Published Nov 9, 2026 3:00 PM EST

A poor sleep schedule doesn’t only affect your overall mood, energy levels, and long-term health. New evidence indicates that losing as little as one hour of rest may increase your chance of falling for an online scam by over 10 percent the following morning. Neurobiologists at the University of California, Irvine, laid out their findings in a study published today in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), arguing that even minimal sleep disruptions can have almost immediate consequences.

“Our results demonstrate that even though you may not be aware of it, lack of sleep leads to impulsive choices, and you may lose more than you gain from putting sleep on the back burner,” said UC Irvine neurobiologist and study co-author Eitan Schechtman.

If you have already fallen prey to a scam email in the past, you can at least take some small comfort in the knowledge that you aren’t alone. Cybercrimes continue to increase exponentially in the United States. The FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center received over one million reports in 2025—a nearly 25 percent increase from only five years earlier.

Remaining aware of con artist tactics and staying up-to-date on personal cybersecurity strategies are some of the best ways to protect yourself. However, Schechtman and his colleagues recently wondered if something as seemingly inconsequential as a single evening of bad sleep may also put people at risk for schemes like an email phishing attack. To investigate, the team partnered with a large, unnamed company as it ran a cybersecurity awareness campaign for more than 11,000 employees. Multiple times a year, the company’s IT department issued emails imitating phishing attempts, then tallied how many workers clicked through the fake malicious links. Schechtman’s team then analyzed results both before the switch to Daylight Saving Time (DST), as well as the Monday after employees lost an hour of sleep.

On the Monday prior to DST, workers clicked on a phishing email link about 15.5 percent. of the time. Then, the Monday immediately following DST saw that rate rise to about 17.7 percent. That may not seem like much, but the difference comes out to about a 13 percent increase in phishing victims after losing approximately just one hour of sleep. According to Schechtman, there are multiple ways to contextualize these results.

“First, they give us a peek into the effects of very minor sleep loss… [from] Daylight Saving Time, which is similar in scope to the kind of sleep loss that many of us experience daily,” he said. “Although we focused on cybersecurity, many of our day-to-day decisions are likely compromised in similar ways.”

Schechtman hopes both employers and cybersecurity companies take regularly sleep-depriving events like DST, holidays, and even primetime sporting events into consideration when advising the public on phishing awareness. In the meantime, he stressed that even those who regularly suffer from sleep issues continue to prioritize their rest as much as possible.

“Better sleep likely leads to better decisions,” he added.

#4565. GM Patents Launch Control That Watches the Drag Strip Christmas Tree, Launches for You

The recent patent describes a system that manages the brakes and throttle to deliver remarkably consistent drag strip blasts away from the line.

Getting a great launch at the drag strip takes more than horsepower and sticky tires. Drivers also need to time their start perfectly; even a tenth of a second can make a difference. Now, General Motors has patented technology that could take that last bit of human involvement out of the equation entirely.

The system uses the vehicle's cameras to watch the drag strip's Christmas Tree, predict when the light will turn green, and launch the car automatically. Better yet, it can actually begin preparing the launch before the green light illuminates. We might be about to see the age of push-button drag racing.

The technology is detailed in U.S. Patent 12,780,203, titled “Methods and Systems for Coordinating Launch Control for Vehicles for Racing.” Originally filed in January 2025, the application was published in July 2026 before finally receiving its patent grant on November 3.

At its core, the system builds on the launch control technology already available in modern performance cars. Right now, most launch control systems work very similarly: the driver applies full brakes and full throttle, and holds both pedals until it's time to go; they let off the brake, and the car rockets away. GM's proposed technology takes over most of that process.

The craziest bit is just how it manages all of this. First, it uses on-board cameras to identify the Christmas tree at the drag strip. Once it recognizes the lights, it notifies the driver and prompts them to activate launch control. Those who want to try this new method could control it much the same as they do with existing systems; the patent describes drivers putting their feet on both pedals and then, once the automatic launch system takes over, the driver can remove both feet and let the car work.

The car can maintain braking pressure and staging torque automatically, even after the driver releases the pedals. The clever part comes next: rather than simply waiting for the green light, the software identifies the sequence of yellow lights and compares it against stored timing patterns to calculate precisely when the race will begin.

That's key, because different events run the lights at different times. For example, a Pro Tree illuminates all three amber lights simultaneously before turning green 0.4 seconds later, whereas Sportsman Tree illuminates the amber lights sequentially with half-second intervals. GM's system could account for those differences automatically. The system is even capable of calculating the delay between commanding movement from the vehicle and the vehicle actually moving forward.

That all said, this is just a patent for now. GM doesn't mention any specific vehicle or plan for production in its filing. If it does bring it to market, we'd be eager to see how close it can come to cutting a perfect light.

The Recon employs a 400-volt electric architecture and is capable of charging from 20 to 80 percent in a claimed 28 minutes on a DC fast charger. Level 2 charging on a 240-volt circuit should take the battery from 5 to 80 percent in roughly 7 hours. The Recon comes standard with many safety and assistance features, including adaptive cruise control, lane-keeping assistance, a 360-degree surround camera, and parking assist.

#4563. Baby chimpanzees blow ‘raspberries’ because adults do it first

Published Nov 9, 2026 3:00 PM EST

The old adage “monkey see, monkey do,” appears to have a bit of truth to it. Chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes) likely watch adults making different vocalization to learn how and when to use those sounds themselves, particularly when they purse their lips to blow “raspberries.” The findings detailed in a study published today in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) show that the primates’ sounds are not instinctual and set in stone, as previously believed.

Humans learn what words mean from the world around us, and different communities will use different sounds for the same thing. For example, English speakers mimic dogs with “woof,” while French speakers say “ouaf.” When it comes to our primate relatives, biologists generally used to believe that they didn’t learn sounds from one another, and that instead biology dictated their sounds. However, that’s changing with some new research into two groups of Chimpanzees in a couple of west African countries.

To probe how chimpanzees learn to use sounds, the study’s team focused on the raspberry. Chimpanzees make this unvoiced sound that’s similar to how humans push their lips together to blow raspberries. The team looked at how 91 chimpanzees, from birth to 55 years old, used the raspberry call. They studied a group of wild chimpanzees from four communities in Taï National Park, Ivory Coast, and a group of young, orphaned, and peer-raised chimpanzees at Tacugama Chimpanzee Sanctuary in Sierra Leone.

The team found that the wild Ivory Coast chimpanzees almost exclusively used the raspberry while grooming others. However, the juveniles at the Tacugama Chimpanzee Sanctuary used it across a much wider range of social situations.

If blowing a raspberry is only an instinctive call, the groups should be using it in similar ways no matter where they were raised. According to the team, these differences suggest that chimpanzees learn from adults how to make a call, as well as when and why to use it.

“In everyday communication, we use the words that we do only because our peers do too. It’s communal practice that fixes their meaning, rather than features of the words themselves,” Richard Moore, a study co-author and mind, language, and psychology philosopher at the University of Warwick, said in a statement.

“The discovery that this is true not just for natural languages but also some chimpanzee calls means there’s more continuity between chimpanzees’ vocal learning and our own than we previously suspected.”

The team also say that when an adult chimpanzee was introduced to one of the groups living in the Tacugama sanctuary, the young chimps gradually began to use the raspberry more consistently and began to resemble the adult’s noises. This suggests that adults serve as role models, helping a community settle in on shared communication patterns.

The researchers say this is the first time that this kind of learned and agreed-upon sound use has been shown in chimpanzee calls. The link between the raspberry sound and its use appears to be shared from one chimpanzee to another, and is not built in at birth. While chimpanzees struggle to learn entirely new call sounds, the study suggests that they can learn the meaning behind sounds that they already know how to make but didn’t use in the same way as other chimps.

“Even aspects of chimpanzee vocal communication that seemed fixed and unlearned may be shaped by learning, suggesting that there is still much to discover about their vocal repertoire,”

added Antoine Valet, a study co-author and cognitive scientist at the Institute of Cognitive Sciences (CNRS) in France.

Additionally, the team has some theories on why different chimpanzee populations use the raspberry in similar ways if it is a learned sound.

“One possibility is that, whilst grooming, as chimpanzees use their lips to extract parasites from another’s fur, it may be easier to generate a vocalisation that uses similar lip movements, a call that is known to prolong grooming bouts,” explained study co-author and CNRS behavioral ecologist Catherine Crockford. “Communities may have found this useful independently, but that wouldn’t change the fact that the call is a convention. We need more research to test it.”

BYD’s luxury brand, Denza, calls it “the king of large 5-seater pure electric vehicles.” The new Denza N8 electric SUV will launch next week, offering an impressive CLTC driving range of over 1,000 km (621 miles), massive digital screens, and plenty of premium extras.

After opening pre-orders for the new 5-seat luxury electric SUV last week, Li Hui, Denza’s general manager, said the results so far “have been excellent.”

According to Li, the Denza N8 is “definitely the most anticipated luxury SUV of the year.” Using BYD’s second-generation Blade Batteries, the Denza N8 EV has a pure electric CLTC range of up to 1,003 km (623 miles) on a single charge.

That’s just as much as the N8 plug-in hybrid (PHEV) it’s replacing, which offered a combined CLTC range of 1,003 km (623 miles) on a full tank of gas and a full charge.

While Li confirmed last week that the new EV variant would go on sale in November, he didn’t give a specific date.

Now, it’s official. Denza announced on its Weibo page on Friday that the launch event for the Denza N8 EV will be held on November 12, 2026.

BYD is still offering a limited-time promo that includes a 5,000 RMB credit for those who place a reservation with a 2,000 RMB ($200) deposit.

The Denza N8 measures 5,150 mm long, 1,999 mm wide, and 1,820 mm high, with a 3,075 mm wheelbase. That’s slightly longer than the Kia EV9 and Hyundai IONIQ 9.

It’s available with a single rear-wheel-drive (RWD) or a tri-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) powertrain. The RWD version uses a single motor producing either 320 kW (429 hp) or 370 kW (496 hp).

The tri-motor Denza N8 uses BYD’s e3 platform. The setup includes three electric motors: a 270 kW (362 hp) front motor and two 310 kW (416 hp) rear motors, for a combined output of 890 kW (1,193 hp).

Regulatory filings earlier this year revealed it will use either a 130.15 kWh or 105.79 kWh BYD Blade 2.0 battery, offering a CLTC range of up to 1,003 km (623 miles) and 800 km (497 miles), respectively.

The Denza N8 also features BYD’s latest Flash Charging technology, letting it recharge from 10% to 80% in just five minutes. It takes just nine minutes to go from 10% to 97%.

Inside, the five-seat electric SUV features a massive 30″ infotainment screen that spans nearly the entire passenger-side dashboard, plus a new 43″ (1.1 meter) panoramic head-up display (PHUD) at the bottom of the windshield.

Like most of its new luxury vehicles, the Denza N8 is loaded with BYD’s latest software and technology.

Added premium features include zero-gravity seating in all rows, a three-spoke steering wheel, wireless phone chargers, and ambient lighting.

The electric SUV is equipped with a roof-mounted LiDAR to support BYD’s God’s Eye 5.0 intelligent driving assistance system, plus its DiSus-A intelligent air suspension system.

BYD has yet to announce prices for the Denza N8 EV, but it will likely be slightly less than the N8L, an extended version that starts at 299,800 RMB ($45,000).

#4561. The Toyota GR GT3 Is Heading to Its First Race This Weekend at Motegi

The Toyota supercar is making its race debut in the Super GT series in Japan.

At long last, the Toyota GR GT3—the racing version of the new GR GT supercar—is officially hitting the racetrack. Seen here in photos at Motegi Circuit outside of Tokyo, the number 32 Eneos X Prime GR GT3 is taking part in the final round of the Super GT sports car racing series in Japan.

Up until now, we’ve only seen the GR GT3 in Toyota’s all-black reveal spec. Now, we finally get to see it dressed in proper race trim, and at the track where it belongs. It has Eneos (a Japanese petroleum company) as the title sponsor, and it wears a bright and colorful orange and red livery with yellow accents aplenty. To say the design is eye-catching would be an understatement.

Rookie Racing team is fielding the car. In case you weren’t familiar, the team shares about as close ties as one car with Toyota, as it’s owned and backed by Akio Toyoda himself. Typically, the team would be fielding a Mercedes-AMG GT3 car, but it’s swapped out this GR GT3 for the double-header event at Motegi this week. It will be the first wheel-to-wheel action the GR GT3 is put through in a racing series.

As of now, we’re expecting the GR GT3 to show up in the U.S. at some point during the 2027 IMSA season; then, the road car is scheduled to launch toward the end of next year. For now, we’re left to drool over these incredible photos of the race car hitting the track for the first time. More photos and videos will surely arrive as the week turns into the weekend, so keep an eye out for updates from Rookie Racing to see more.

#4560. Human sacrifices were rare in ancient Peru, except when weather got violent

Published Nov 9, 2026 5:00 PM EST

Today’s cataclysmic climate change-fueled disasters are scary enough even when we understand the root causes. Prehistoric cultures unfortunately didn’t have this luxury, and often responded dramatically to such changes. In northern Peru, archaeological evidence indicates local societies sometimes even turned to mass human sacrifices in an attempt to stop destructive flooding from events like El Niño.

That said, researchers are now confident these periods of intense violence weren’t the norm—nor were they necessarily linked to climate issues. According to their study recently published in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology, such brutal moments were actually pretty rare occurrences in Peru’s Lambayeque Valley.

“The main thing that jumped out at us was just how few cases of interpersonal violence we observed outside ritualized contexts,” said New York University archaeologist and study co-author Thomas Snyder.

The Lambayeque Valley is located inside northern Peru’s coastal desert, but the region has hosted residents for  6,000 years. Although the valley generally receives little rainfall, its rivers and proximity to the sea allowed communities to flourish there for generations, including societies like the Moche from roughly 100–750 CE, and the Sicán from about 750–1375 CE.

“Archaeological evidence shows that in so many ways they were mirrors of us—in how they lived their daily lives, interacted with their world, ran their economies, and confronted (and sometimes contributed to) environmental crises,” explained George Mason University archaeologist and study co-author Haagen Klaus.

Previous excavations have indicated that mass human sacrifices possibly preceded the collapse of the Moche and Sicán’s political systems. Researchers have since hypothesized that these acts likely coincided with periods of mass flooding,probably due to El Niño weather oscillations. Just like today, these weather events destroyed food stocks and disrupted agricultural production. Since large human sacrificial rituals may have been attempts by the ruling class to restore balance to nature, the team to wonder if violence was simply a more common facet of everyday life for the Moche and Sicán.

“If these big ritual sacrifices were indicative of some underlying crisis, we hypothesized that these events might have been extending into people’s everyday experience of the world,” said Snyder.

Klaus, Snyder, and their collaborators turned to the Lambayeque Valley Biohistory Project’s skeletal archive for answers. The collection spans about 3,000 years of history across 30 different archaeological sites. The team established relatively precise death estimates for over 1,600 individuals, while also examining them for evidence of intentional cranial trauma associated with human sacrifice. Contrary to their theory, only 25 remains (1.6 percent of the sample pool) showed signs of violence, while just 77 displayed indicators of accidental trauma. Of those, none were directly linked to known periods of past ecological crises.

“In Lambayeque, there’s 6,000 years of creative adaptations to El Niño and longer-term changes in climate, and widespread violence wasn’t one of them,” concluded Klaus.

The study’s authors noted that because they were notable to radiocarbon date all of the remains, their findings remain broader estimates of wide time periods. At the same time, they stressed the evidence underscores humanity’s history of facing intense climate challenges not with violence, but adaptation.

“This really highlights that widespread violence isn’t a predetermined response to climate change,” said Snyder. “As a society, we both get to and have to choose how we respond to our own climate crisis.”

“Violence and social unraveling are not destined outcomes, ever,” added Klaus.

#4559. EVgo opens its first Tesla Superchargers, with hundreds more planned

EVgo has opened its first Supercharger station, and it’s in a Chicago grocery store parking lot. The site has 12 fast-charging stalls with both NACS and CCS plugs, and it’s the first of hundreds of Tesla Supercharger stalls EVgo plans to add across the US.

The 325 kW “EVgo Superchargers” are at Riverside Square & River’s Edge, at 3145 S Ashland Avenue. EVgo’s August announcement cited up to 500 kW for the Supercharger rollout.

The Chicago location features Magic Dock technology, which means both NACS and CCS vehicles can charge without an adapter. Drivers of compatible non-Tesla EVs can start a session through the Tesla app. If you drive a Tesla, the charging station shows up in the car’s navigation and Trip Planner. Other EVgo fast chargers with NACS plugs have been showing up in Tesla navigation since early September if you turn on third-party charging.

“By serving both Tesla and non-Tesla NACS drivers, we’re doubling EVgo’s addressable market and continuing to meet EV drivers where they are and where they want to charge,” said Badar Khan, EVgo CEO.

EVgo owns the Superchargers and self-brands them, and Tesla runs and maintains them. The first sites will be at Regency Centers shopping plazas with grocery stores.

Smart move on EVGo's part. More reliable charger at a lower cost than they can build themselves, and Tesla takes on all the maintenance and network operations for a slice of the sales.

EVgo is also adding NACS plugs to its regular fast-charging network, a rollout it started in 2025. The company aims to have 500 of those stalls across the US by the end of 2026, with Supercharger stalls counted separately. Over the next two years, it plans to put at least one NACS plug at every EVgo site built in 2023 or later.

#4557. Hyundai’s $359 IONIQ 5 lease looks like a deal, but don’t overlook its bigger sibling

The Hyundai IONIQ 5 is the most popular EV in America outside of Tesla, but its larger three-row sibling looks like the better deal right now.

Through September, the Hyundai IONIQ 5 was the third top-selling EV in the US, behind the Tesla Model Y and Model 3.

Hyundai’s electric SUV is outselling rivals like the Chevy Equinox EV, Ford Mustang Mach-E, and Toyota bZ.

Why? For one, it’s one of the most affordable EVs in the US, starting at about $35,000, and Hyundai has been offering some of the most attractive lease deals.

After the $7,500 federal EV tax credit expired at the end of September last year, Hyundai responded by reducing prices on the IONIQ 5 by up to nearly $10,000 on some trims.

The 2027 Hyundai IONIQ 5 starts at $35,250. That’s for the standard-range IONIQ 5 SE with an EPA-estimated range of up to 245 miles. Upgrading to the extended-range SE RWD model adds $2,500, starting at $37,750, and offers up to 318 miles of range.

Hyundai’s three-row electric SUV, the IONIQ 9, starts at $58,955, or nearly $24,000 more than the base IONIQ 5 SE.

On Hyundai’s website, the 2027 IONIQ 5 SE Standard Range is available to lease from $359 a month. The offer is for a 24-month lease with $4,999 due at signing for an effective cost of $567 per month.

The extended-range Hyundai IONIQ 5 SE RWD can be leased from $369 a month. The offer is also a 24-month lease with $4,999 due at signing, for an effective cost of $577 per month.

Hyundai’s larger IONIQ 9, meanwhile, is available to lease from $419 a month. That deal also includes $4,999 due at signing, but is for a 36-month lease, so the effective cost is $557 per month.

Using Hyundai’s payment calculator, it would cost about $412 a month to lease the 2027 Hyundai IONIQ 5 SE for 36 months with $4,999 due at signing. With an effective cost of $550 per month, it’s only $7 less than the three-row IONIQ 9.

The Hyundai IONIQ 9 offers more range than its smaller sibling, with an EPA-estimated range of up to 335 miles for the base SE trim.

The IONIQ 5 is a midsize electric SUV, about the same size as a Tesla Model Y, with two rows and enough room for five passengers. Hyundai’s larger IONIQ 9 offers three rows of seating and six- or seven-seat configurations.

With an added row of seating, the IONIQ 9 offers up to 163.54 cubic feet of interior passenger volume, compared with the IONIQ 5, which offers up to 106.5 cubic feet.

While the IONIQ 9 may be the better deal right now, the IONIQ 5 is still a good fit for those looking for a smaller, more efficient SUV that doesn’t necessarily need the added space.

In comparison, the standard Tesla Model Y RWD is listed for lease starting at $499 a month with an EPA range of up to 321 miles. That’s for a 36-month lease with $3,000 down.

Using Tesla’s payment calculator, if you put the same $4,999 down for a 24-month lease like the IONIQ 5, the Model Y RWD’s monthly rate is $549.

Which one would you choose? The IONIQ 5, IONIQ 9, or Tesla Model Y? Let us know why in the comments.

Both the IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9 are built at Hyundai’s Metaplant America outside of Savannah, Georgia.

I really haven’t seen much value in leasing. I’d rather buy the car outright using cash, with the goal of keeping the car for 10+ years.

My family recently bought a Hyundai IONIQ 5, and it is an outstanding car. Loaded with great features — both on the EV side and then for safety and comfort.

When we toured the facility earlier this year, Hyundai told us that its electric SUVs are attracting new buyers to the brand at a higher rate than its gas or hybrid vehicles.

The IONIQ 5 had a 69.8% conquest rate last year, while the IONIQ 9 had 64.3%. Hyundai’s Elantra N ranked third (61.9%), followed by the Palisade (61.2%) and Kona Electric (60.9%).

Hyundai’s current offers end on November 30, 2026. Want to see what’s available near you? You can use the links below to find available Hyundai IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9 models near you, along with any current offers.

#4555. The Most Expensive Ford Fathom Electric Truck Will Still Start Under $40,000: Report

The Ford Fathom will arrive for the 2028 model year in multiple trim levels, according to the Detroit Free Press, but they’ll all be reasonably priced.

Ford’s new affordable mid-size electric truck was announced earlier this year, and company executives are now hinting at how much even the nicest Fathom pickup will cost, according to The Detroit Free Press.

We already know a base model Ford Fathom will start at $29,945, including a $1595 destination charge. But Andrew Frick, president of Ford’s Model e division, told the Detroit Free Press that even a fully-loaded Fathom won’t crest $40,000. That’s some serious value for a truck that is set to offer a touchscreen, built-in Apple Maps, Apple CarPlay, Android Auto, and Blue Cruise hands-free driving capabilities.

"We'll have a range that goes to the high $30,000 range.  And we'll have a couple different offerings within that," said to the Detroit Free Press. "If you know that nearly fifty percent of the U.S. new vehicle industry transacts under $40,000, not only do we expect Fathom ... to attract new and used EV buyers, but also (gasoline) and hybrid customers, especially because we're going to have much lower operating costs than even a mainstream hybrid vehicle."

Ford CEO Jim Farley was duly impressed during a test drive of the Fathom. "It completely blew me away. Zero to sixty is huge … and the hands-free experience was like something I've never experienced. Fathom is really a breakthrough product. It's highly capable, innovative, affordable,” Farley said during a Wall Street analyst meeting on October 28.

Designers at Ford told Road & Track earlier this year that the Fathom will be spacious, too, as the four-door pickup will have more passenger volume than a Toyota RAV4. Additionally, the truck is being used to pilot a new “Universal EV Production System” at its Louisville Assembly Plant in Kentucky. With over $2 billion invested in retooling the plant, Ford is betting big on the new production process and its 400-volt Universal EV platform, which will launch with the Fathom.

Details about the Fathom’s powertrain and specific trim levels have yet to be announced. The all-electric pickup truck is set to arrive in late 2027, but pre-orders will open in the first quarter of that year.

A New York transplant hailing from the Pacific Northwest, Emmet White has a passion for anything that goes: cars, bicycles, planes, and motorcycles. After learning to ride at 17, Emmet worked in the motorcycle industry before joining Autoweek in 2022 and Road & Track in 2024. The woes of alternate side parking have kept his fleet moderate, with a 2014 Volkswagen Jetta GLI and a BMW 318i E30 street parked in his Queens community.

#4553. Apollo’s newest electric scooter is also its lowest-cost yet

Apollo has spent the last several years carving out a spot for itself toward the more premium end of the electric scooter market. Now the company is trying something different: going after the mass market with its least expensive model yet.

The new Apollo Dash carries a $699 MSRP, but is launching at $599 as part of the company’s Black Friday sale running through November 30. More importantly, Apollo says the Dash isn’t intended to simply be a stripped-down budget scooter, but rather a way to bring much of its existing technology down to a lower price point.

The scooter uses a 48V electrical system powering a 600W nominal, 1,200W peak-rated Bosch motor, with a top speed of 20 mph (32 km/h). Its 480Wh battery is rated for up to 25 miles (40 km) of range in Eco mode.

Apollo also claims the 48V architecture avoids limiting motor power to anemic levels as the battery drains, meaning riders shouldn’t experience the same increasingly sluggish performance toward the bottom of the battery that can occur on some lower-cost scooters.

At 43 lb (19.5 kg), the Dash is reasonably portable, though getting the weight and price down comes with an important compromise: there’s no suspension. Apollo also caps rider weight at 220 lb (100 kg), and points heavier riders or those regularly tackling rough roads and hills toward the more expensive Apollo Go instead.

Despite the lower price, there’s still a surprisingly long feature list. The Dash gets IP66 water resistance, self-healing tubeless tires, regenerative braking, built-in turn signals, Apollo’s Beam stem light, NFC unlocking, Apple Find My integration, and connectivity with the Apollo smartphone app.

Apollo says it put the frame through 10,000 km (6,200 miles) of durability validation before shipping production units. A beta test program also accumulated 1,002 miles over 144 rides without any reported punctures or maintenance issues. Beta riders averaged 19 miles (30 km) per ride while finishing with 29% battery remaining, according to Apollo.

Perhaps the bigger story here, though, is where Apollo is positioning the Dash. The company says 52% of its customers previously owned scooters from brands including Segway, NIU, and Xiaomi, but historically moving up to an Apollo often meant crossing the $1,000 mark.

At $599, the Dash appears designed to get those riders into Apollo’s ecosystem much earlier – while also putting the company squarely into competition with the mass-market scooters it previously sat above.

And for those wanting a bit more power or features, Apollo’s more upmarket models are on sale now as part of early Black Friday promotions.

#4551. Honda’s HRC Performance Parts Business Was a Long Time Coming

Oh, and the Civic Type R HRC concept? Yeah, it’s gonna be sold here in the United States.

Honda has made no secret of its plans to eventually enter the performance parts business with HRC-branded components. This is part of a larger campaign to turn the HRC brand—now the global name for all Honda motorsports activities—into a performance footprint on par with Nissan’s Nismo or BMW’s M. And like those brands, it sure seems like complete production models will be sold with that performance badge, too.

Both HRC performance parts and HRC road cars were a hot topic at the 2026 SEMA Show, where the company showed off race cars, custom builds, and one very interesting concept. In an interview with Road & Track, HRC U.S. senior vice president Jon Ikeda made it clear that the Civic Type R HRC concept on display (seen below) was “going to be sold here.”

“We’ve shared with everyone that it’s coming here,” Ikeda added, “and we’re really excited about it. We have big debuts coming next year—at the Tokyo Auto Salon, a big debut there. We’re just happy that our region is included; there are a lot of people who are excited about it here.”

While he stopped short of confirming similar plans for an Acura Integra Type S HRC, Ikeda noted that consumer interest is strong and suggested that the company “[has] to seriously think about doing it.”

An HRC Integra may not be a lock, but Honda has already confirmed that the four-door Acura will join the Civic Type R in receiving performance parts offered directly by HRC. Ikeda notes that the Integra’s offerings will include wheels from 2Elle, the supplier of the forged wheels used on the recently-retired ARX-06 race car. Those, and other components, were tested on an Integra Type S at the Nürburgring Nordschleife ahead of the SEMA showcase. Ikeda mentions the value of these parts being sold directly by the OEM—a major distinction that keeps options open for owners worried about voiding a warranty or decreasing a car’s resale value.

“As soon as you accessorize,” he continues, “you void your warranty on things. If you own a Honda car, you do a third party purchase of a spring or something, you devalue your vehicle. By creating OEM parts, you’re able to honor the warranty when you buy the car, you can even finance it, bundle it up in your financing if you want if you do it at the dealership. If you have all the OEM parts to upgrade, it’s not a new business framework. Others are doing it. We have a very equitable brand to say, ‘hey, you’ve got OEM HRC parts, put it on your car, get your warranty, don’t devalue your vehicle, enjoy the ride.’ That’s a big, big part of it.”

HRC parts will begin arriving at dealers in the first quarter of next year. The HRC-badged Civic Type R should be revealed at the Tokyo Auto Salon in January.

#4550. View Exterior Photos of the 2027 Karma Gyesera Grand Coupe

See the exterior of the Karma Gyesera Grand Coupe from every angle.

Read the Full Review | See Interior Photos

The 2027 Karma Gyesera is the latest evolution of the plug-in hybrid sedan that first arrived as the Fisker Karma way back in 2011, and it gets a revised powertrain and design as Karma Automotive aims to kick off a new era.

The Gyesera has the same dramatic proportions as its forebears, with a long hood and a curvaceous body, built around an evolution of the aluminum spaceframe chassis found in the Revero that it replaces.

The body is fashioned from a mix of aluminum and carbon fiber, helping keep the curb weight at just over 5000 pounds despite the Gyesera’s lengthy silhouette.

The Gyesera employs the fifth generation of Karma’s plug-in hybrid system, which uses a BMW turbocharged three-cylinder engine as a generator to maintain the charge of a 28-kWh battery.

That battery is hooked up to a pair of electric motors mounted on the rear axle, and the Gyesera produces 566 horsepower and 594 pound-feet of torque.

That’s 30 more horses and 44 more pound-feet than its predecessor, the Revero, allowing the Gyesera to hit 60 mph in a claimed 3.7 seconds and a top speed of 150 mph.

Karma says the battery provides an electric-only driving range of 80 miles; once the gas engine kicks off, range extends to 360 miles.

#4549. Amazon set to deploy more than 3,000 TATA electric delivery trucks

Amazon isn’t just electrifying its American delivery operations. The virtual big box stores that Bezos built understands the benefits of EVs as well as anyone, and they’re working hard to deploy electric vehicles everywhere they can. And now, that global push is extending to India.

Indian automaker TATA Motors has announced a deal with Amazon to deploy 3,000 electric trucks across Amazon’s transportation network in India. When it goes live, it will be the largest electric truck deployment by in India and mark Amazon’s most significant move to extend its Indian fleet electrification beyond last-mile logistics.

“India is accelerating towards electric mobility and the realization of Viksit Bharat 2047,” says Shri H.D. Kumaraswamy, Hon’ble Union Minister for Heavy Industries and Steel, Government of India. “The collaboration between TATA Motors and Amazon shows what that looks like in practice: sustained demand from a nationwide logistics network met by electric trucks manufactured in India. Through PM E-DRIVE, the Government will continue to support this transition, and I look forward to more such efforts in powering green logistics.”

In addition to being a big deal for TATA, the 3,000 electric truck deal represents a serous bump to India’s deployed electric truck fleet, and are a major step towards the wide-scale electrification of freight transportation across the country – that’s not just good for Amazon’s fuel bills, it’s good for everyone and everything that breathes air, too.

“Electrifying our logistics and transportation network is an important part of Amazon’s goal to achieve net-zero carbon emissions by 2040,” says Abhinav Singh, Vice President, Operations, Amazon, APAC, Middle East, Africa and Turkey. “We have made significant progress in India, with more than 15,000 electric vehicles operating across 500-plus cities. To enable this transition, we are also supporting the development of infrastructure and solutions that make EV adoption easier for our carrier partners and drivers. We are now setting a bold vision to scale electric trucking, addressing one of the toughest challenges in decarbonizing transportation. Our collaboration with TATA Motors marks an important step towards realizing this vision. By combining our strengths, we aim to accelerate the deployment of electric trucks across more routes, starting with intracity operations and expanding to India’s major freight corridors.”

The truck Amazon will be deploying in these record numbers is a version of the Tata Ultra E.7, a 7.5-tonne (~16,000 lb.) straight truck powered by a 240 kW (~320 hp) electric motor drawing power from a 96 kWh LFP battery pack. The truck’s makers claim a loaded range of up to 130 km (~80 miles) on a single charge, with DC fast-charging that’s capable enough to keep the trucks charged up between deliveries.

Amazon’s new TATA electric delivery trucks will support the transport of goods between warehouse facilities – which means traveling across cities and along India’s national freight corridors.

#4548. In medieval Italy, a spider bite could send you into a dancing frenzy

Published Nov 10, 2026 9:01 AM EST

There’s a chance that if you visited southern Italy during the Middle Ages, you might happen upon a port town where people were dancing uncontrollably in the streets. You’d find them frantically spinning, jumping…even crawling on the ground. But unlike the broader “dancing mania” that was taking place across Europe at the same time, this dance, dubbed the “tarantella,” was more than a sickness. It was also a cure.

“Some people say that the bite of a spider caused people to tremor and shake,” Anna Harsh, a professional dancer and founder of the Allegro Dance Company, which specializes in Italian folk dances, tells Popular Science. They’d then continue moving to sweat out the poison.

Tarantism, a historical psychological and social phenomenon that led to anxiety, melancholia, and uncontrollable movement, ran rapidly throughout southern Italy from the 11th to the 17th century.

The epicenter of tarantism was Taranto, a coastal city in southern Italy’s Puglia region, which occupies the “heel” of the country’s boot shape. Each summer harvest season, local residents would spend long days working in the fields where large, hairy wolf spiders burrowed.

Most people believed that these wolf spiders carried a toxic venom. If they bit you, tarantism would quickly set in. The only cure would be to sweat out the venom through continuous, fast-paced dancing. We’re talking uncontrollable, flailing movements that would eventually exhaust both the dancer and the illness.

Although southern Italy was the epicenter of tarantism, similar outbreaks of involuntary, convulsive dancing occurred throughout the Middle Ages. The first major recorded frenzy began on June 24, 1374 in Aachen, Germany. Soon after, others followed in countries like Switzerland and modern-day France. In many of these cases, those afflicted danced uncontrollably for days or weeks. Some even died dancing. Since these events happened centuries ago, no one really knows what caused them. But the tarantism of southern Italy and its ensuing tarantella dance both seem unique.

The name “tarantula” may have originated with the wolf spiders (Lycosa tarantula) of Taranto, but wolf spiders and tarantulas belong to two entirely different spider families. Still, with a leg span that can reach up to three to four inches across, multiple sets of eyes, and a series of odd, jerky movements when they walk, wolf spiders make easy targets for conspiracy theories and urban legends.

While they can look frightening, science has determined over the years that a wolf spider’s bite is generally harmless to humans. Symptoms appear more like a mild bee sting, with a bit of localized pain and swelling, then a full-blown disco dance party. In fact, among the world’s 38,000 known spider species, only about 100 species have venom that is detrimental to humans.

In 1976, a college paper blamed the Salem witch trials on moldy bread. It wasn’t true.

Ancient Romans thought drinking gladiator blood could cure epilepsy

In medieval France, murderous pigs faced trial and execution

4 times drinking coffee was illegal—or even punishable by death

In August 1693, an anonymous Neapolitan doctor even tested the connection between the bite of a wolf spider and tarantism. He let two wolf spiders bite him in a public experiment, but the doctor never broke out into fancy footwork.

Instead, modern science shows that the extreme summer heat, physical stress, dehydration, and even ample wine drinking could have easily caused the symptoms of tarantism. Still, the wolf spider and tarantism remain undisputedly linked.

Sometimes called the “Dance of the Spider,” the tarantella began as a ritual healing dance that aimed to sweat out any venom associated with tarantism. Many versions of the tarantella exist today, though they’re more traditional folk dances than medical treatments. Instead, the  ‘tarantella as cure’ dance is more formally known as the pizzica. The word pizzica comes from the Italian verb pizzicare, which means “to pinch” or “to bite.”

“Today we might think of that ‘bite’ as something internal, like stress or anxiety,” says Harsh. Picture when someone you know suddenly loses a loved one and they’re shaking uncontrollably. “That person will dance or move and do whatever they can to help them get through that situation.”

Pizzica tarantata is performed almost like an exorcism, the spiritual practice of evicting demons or malevolent entities (such as supposed spider’s venom) through a sort of ritual—in this case, ecstatic, free-form dance.

Musicians gathered around the inflicted victim, playing incessant, fast-paced 6/8-tempo rhythms driven by a tambourine, violins, and guitars. The person suffering from tarantism would then “go into a trance,” says Harsh. “There was shaking, hopping, swirling, and turning. Some people would roll on the ground and come back up. The pizzica has movements, but you can put them in any order. It’s however the spirit moves you.”

These days, most historians and scientists agree that wolf spiders didn’t cause tarantism. Rather, tarantism was a form of mass hysteria, a situation where a group of people share the same intense fear, anxiety, or physical sickness—like dizziness, shaking, or stomach aches—even though there is no real physical or medical grounds for it.

Tarantism mostly afflicted impoverished individuals, particularly women (tarantatas). One possible reason: “Women were oppressed and faced plenty of inequality,” says Harsh. “Dance is a way that they could express themselves, even scream, through movement. That they could be the center of attention for just a minute and be seen.”

Over the centuries, the tarantella has become a celebration of life and joy rather than a frantic ritual. Italians often perform this now-beloved folk dance at weddings and festivals.

Every August, La Notte della Taranta, Europe’s largest open-air festival dedicated to traditional folk music, the pizzica, and the tarantella, takes place in Italy’s Puglia region.

Whether or not dancing works to sweat out a toxic venom, studies do show that dancing helps reduce stress and increases levels of serotonin, a hormone that helps regulate mood, sleep, and digestion.

“You know, whatever is biting at us, whether it’s grief or loss, we can move together, follow the rhythm of a drummer, and heal ourselves in a sense,” says Harsh. “The movement just takes over and we stop thinking about our troubles.”

Though if you do endure a lethal spider bite, we’d recommend the ER over two-stepping.

#4547. Tested: 2027 Mercedes-AMG GT 55 4-Door Proves EVs Can Be Engaging

This is an electric car that makes V-8 noises, goes like stink, and is loaded to the gills with Mercedes luxury.

Making a performance EV compelling enough to convince enthusiasts to jump on board has proven difficult, but that’s precisely what Mercedes-AMG is trying to do with the 2027 4-Door Coupe. Mercedes is going down the same path as other manufacturers and their acclaimed electric performance machines—such as the Hyundai Ioniq 5 N and Genesis GV60 Magma—by simulating the experience of a car equipped with an internal-combustion engine. It’s great fun, but the efforts would be for naught if the rest of the car didn’t live up to the experience. Thankfully, this electric AMG is a ripper from every angle. Except when viewed from the rear. Maybe avoid doing that.

Our expert editors test every vehicle we review. Read more about how we test and review cars here.

It’s hardly lesser, but the “55” in the AMG GT 55 4-Door Coupe is empirically less mighty than the “63” in the GT 63. This EV features a tri-motor powertrain made up of three axial-flux motors engineered with YASA that combine for 805 hp and 1372 pound-feet of torque. That 805 hp figure is the peak, the lesser “continuous” rating coming in at 557 hp. But if you want all the power, all the time, that can be accomplished by putting the car in Race mode, or pulling both steering-wheel paddles to activate Boost mode, which lasts for 55 seconds. Mercedes claims a 2.7-second 0–60-mph time and top speed of 186 mph should you option the AMG Performance package.

Powertrain layout: 2 rear electric motors, 1 front

Slipping behind the wheel, the first thing that struck me about the GT 55 was the properly low seating position. Excellent work there, Mercedes. After fumbling about with the confusing start/stop button on the stalk (the car doesn’t really turn on until you flick it into Drive or Reverse), I started comfortably trundling along.

The AMG Active Ride Control air suspension did a standup job on the track in the GT 63, but it’s even more remarkable on the road in the 55. An air suspension with adaptive dampers is standard, but this optional hydraulically interconnected damper system is assuredly the one you want. Combined with the multilink suspension in the front and rear, an abundance of forged aluminum components on the front axle, and rear-axle steering up to six degrees, this chassis just oozes confidence right off the bat. There was no jittery stiffness or harshness to the ride in Comfort, and it was only moderately sharper on bumps in the punchier modes. You could spend every day behind the wheel thinking you’re in a regular Mercedes and not an AMG product.

But when I found some sweepers, the front end just begged for me to keep piling on speed thanks to how stable everything feels. At points, it was almost too confidence-inspiring, as the sophisticated chassis was writing checks the GT’s 5501-pound mass and Continental SportContact 7 summer tires struggled to cash on some of southern Spain’s steep downhill slaloms. The steering and body control say go, go, but the tires quickly say they need a break from the heat. Don’t mistake that as a braking system limitation either, because the optional carbon-ceramics hold up to mega abuse. I just wish the pedal feel wasn’t so mushy and inconsistent throughout the stroke.

Accelerating out of corners, the sensation was AMG at its best. With the ESP system in Sport mode, the rear tires surrendered grip progressively and tidily. It was so consistent and predictable that it almost felt calculated, and to a degree, it is. Mercedes let me play with the AMG Race Engineer system in the 63 model on the racetrack—that’s the three dials in the center console which let the driver customize how hairy or locked down they want the experience from a traction control and yaw agility perspective. The 55 has the exact same system, given you option it. It’s fun to toy with on the track but can just as easily change the character of the car on a fast canyon road to suit your mood.

And then there’s AMGForce Sport+, the system that simulates both a V-8 engine and a multi-clutch transmission system and that proved remarkably adept at convincing me I was piloting an internal-combustion-powered car. Mercedes mimics the soundtrack and other theatrics—engine braking, seat vibrations, and shifting—from the previous-gen AMG GT R Coupe. I found myself tapping up and down the paddles through the mountains with glee for miles on end. Yeah, it’s all fake, but the alternative is a pure electric car experience that I find gets a bit boring after a short period.

Would a proper V-8 and real transmission have been more involving and addicting to wind out? Absolutely. But even if you set aside the stagecraft, this AMG is a blast to drive. It toes the line between back-road barn burner and everyday luxury like the very best AMGs of recent history. Plus, the EV hardware backing everything up is elite.

A 106-kWh battery pack developed specifically for AMG performance cars can be charged at speeds over 600 kW, allowing you to go from 10 to 80 percent in only 11 minutes. No, 600-kW chargers don’t exist in the U.S. yet, but when they arrive, this car will be ready. The system can even switch from 800 to 400 volts by virtually “splitting” the pack in half for less compromised charging at 400-volt stations, which should help tremendously at Tesla Superchargers. Range figures aren’t out yet, but Mercedes is claiming up to 434 miles on the optimistic European WLTP test, so you can rest assured that EPA numbers will be well over 300 miles.

Mercedes has clearly done some learning from all the criticism leveled at its interiors over the past half-decade. The GT’s steering wheel has a proper scroll wheel for volume and a switch for cruise control. The door-positioned seat toggles physically move when you press them (finally), and those AMG Race Engineer controls in the center console are aptly the most satisfying knobs to turn in the whole car. The quilted leather on the doors themselves is spectacular, but don’t worry, there’s plenty to wrinkle a brow at too.

Adjusting the heated and ventilated seat controls requires multiple extremely precise stabs at the touchscreen. Trying to find your way around the unending drive mode and sound mode controls will require patience for even the most tech-savvy. And while the massive screens are of superb quality in terms of both picture and response, the sheer amount of real estate dedicated to them could easily be a turn-off. On the plus side, the dedicated tachometer that pops up in Sport+ mode is probably the best digital tach fitted to a Mercedes yet. Ironic that it arrives in an EV.

Practicality doesn’t take a back seat with this long, swoopy liftback. Despite its name, this is a four-door hatchback, and unlike the Porsche Taycan, it has enough space in the rear to seat medium-to-tall adults. It doesn’t completely suck to get in or out either. In another win for the AMG over Porsche’s sport sedan, the 14.7-cubic-foot cargo area seems positively massive. You can extend it further by putting the rear seats down, leaving an impressively large space to go road-tripping or move large items with. A carbon-fiber frunk exists for smaller items, too, and it’s here you’ll find the traditional signed AMG plaque, only this one is signed by any number of folks involved in the design or engineering of the vehicle.

If you found the Taycan a little too serious or not practical enough, the AMG GT 55 4-Door Coupe might be just the EV you’re looking for. It lands in between the Taycan 4S and GTS, but is quicker than both of those Taycan variants in a straight line. The Porsche is the more serious sports car, though practicality is firmly on Mercedes’s side. The debate between the 63 and 55 is where things get a little tricky with about a $30,000 gulf between the two—the 55 starts at $146,500, the 63 at $176,550.

Then there’s the forthcoming fully electric BMW M3 to consider, but we need to wait for pricing on that. But putting that and the GT together already feels as if it will be one of the benchmark tests of 2027.

I didn’t drive the GT 63 on the road, but it didn’t feel significantly quicker than the GT 55 in a straight line. Both have the same overengineered battery pack and tri-motor powertrain. The differences are largely in the suspension and software, like the AMG Race Engineer (again, optional on the 55) and pure luxury features like massage seats and an enormous HUD. That said, when you’re spending $145K and some change for options, what’s another $30,000 to get it all? If extra-dynamic driving isn’t in your future, perhaps a base 55 without all the go-fast goodies makes fiscal sense. But otherwise, it’s hard to imagine anyone who has sold themselves on the idea of the GT 4-Door not wanting the full 63 experience.

The active rear diffuser takes moving aero to a new level of complex and cool. Mercedes says it provides a boost to efficiency on the highway, but it also helps stability at high speeds. Watching it extend and retract on the move is quite the party trick. And thankfully, you can manually extend it to show off to your friends who are stuck with passive rear diffusers on their cars.

#4546. The 2027 Karma Gyesera Is a Stylish Curiosity

The Gyesera replaces the Revero, itself a descendant of the original Fisker Karma, with a sultry design and an updated plug-in hybrid powertrain.

Henrik Fisker probably had no idea how fitting the name Karma would be when he launched the plug-in hybrid sedan in 2011 under his eponymous startup. In Hinduism, karma is intrinsically linked to reincarnation, the karma accumulated in one life affecting the conditions of the next life. Fisker’s venture wound up failing in 2014, but after Wanxiang Group, a Chinese automotive parts conglomerate, bought the assets, the car was reborn as the Karma Revero. The Revero has been built since 2016 and has undergone several updates, but the tiny California-based company has struggled to gain a foothold.

Now Karma Automotive is seeking to reinvent itself, and it will start by giving the plug-in hybrid sedan yet another reincarnation. Marques McCammon—previously of DaimlerChrysler, Roush, Saleen, and engineering firm Ricardo—joined as president of the company in 2023, and the 2027 Gyesera is the first product launched under his guidance. While it retains similarities to the sedans that preceded it, a lightly updated powertrain and a fresh design language aim to set the brand up for a brighter future. Driving a pre-production version of the Gyesera in and around Las Vegas, we discovered a car that feels special and provides enticing powertrain flexibility but that is still bound by some of the same flaws as its predecessors.

See all results for used cars for sale near 50317

The Gyesera was initially revealed in 2024 as a fully electric vehicle, but Karma Automotive pivoted when it determined that the luxury market wasn’t moving toward EVs fast enough. Instead of the originally proposed 590-hp battery-electric setup, the Gyesera now launches with a fifth generation of the Karma’s plug-in hybrid powertrain. A turbocharged 1.5-liter three-cylinder engine—borrowed from the BMW i8—lives under the hood, but it isn’t connected to the wheels. Instead, it acts as a generator to charge the 28-kWh battery, which then feeds electricity to a pair of motors on the rear axle.

The Gyesera produces 566 horsepower—30 hp more than the Revero—and 594 pound-feet of torque, an increase of 44. Karma says the Gyesera accelerates from zero to 60 mph in 3.7 seconds, down from 4.5 seconds in the Revero, and can hit a 150-mph top speed, up from the Revero’s 125-mph V-max. The nickel-manganese-cobalt battery is also capable of providing a claimed 80 miles of electric-only driving, with a total range on gasoline of 360 miles. The battery can support DC fast-charging via a CCS port at up to 50 kilowatts or AC charging at 6.6 kilowatts.

As you approach the Gyesera, it makes a strong first impression. There remains more than a whiff of the original Fisker Karma in its appearance, with the Gyesera using an evolution of the aluminum spaceframe chassis found in previous Karmas. Design-wise, this is no bad thing. The proportions look exotic, with a hood that seems to go on forever and a roofline that tapers over the muscular rear haunches. The curvaceous body is fashioned from a mix of aluminum and carbon fiber, the latter comprising the hood, rear decklid, fenders, rocker panels, and optionally, the roof.

See all results for used cars for sale near 50317

While the shape is familiar, the design has been sharpened. Up front, a crisp line runs underneath piercing headlights, replacing the black grille trim that made the Revero look like an athlete wearing a mouthguard. The lower air intake is framed by a carbon-fiber trim piece, while a swooping indent, which Karma calls the Comet Line, arcs across the hood, giving the car a powerful look and serving as a hot air outlet for the engine bay. A strip of exposed, unpainted carbon fiber at the top of the hood is a reminder of the Gyesera’s high-end construction.

The forged aluminum wheels are the fruit of a partnership with HRE, with two different 21-inch designs available along with a 22-inch option. The smooth sides are broken up by a carbon-fiber trim piece carved into the front fender, and at the rear, slim taillights sit above a subtle diffuser. The Gyesera’s visual drama is even more apparent in person, and even amid the fancy cars in Vegas, the Gyesera turned heads on the Strip.

Inside, Karma revised the dashboard, ditching the Revero’s four circular air vents for rectangular vents hidden within a black trim piece that spans the dash. The 10.1-inch screen has been repositioned and is paired with a 12.3-inch digital gauge cluster. Some things remain unchanged from the Revero, such as the pyramid-like push-button gear selector and the steering wheel, which still has an echo of the original Fisker Karma’s design.

The highlight, though, is the cabin’s luxurious materials. The seats and dashboard feature sumptuous Bridge of Weir leather, while the center console, door armrests, and parts of the steering wheel are covered in soft Alcantara microsuede. The metallic trim feels solid and cool, but the glossy black plastic covering the center console is a low point.

Most functions are handled digitally, but we didn’t find it as infuriating as other screen-focused setups, in part because the screen is within easy reach of the driver. We still believe real buttons and dials feel more upscale, but the screen, which also supports wireless phone mirroring, wasn’t too fussy. To keep your phone topped up, there’s a wireless charger and USB-C ports hidden inside the armrest.

The battery is housed in what would traditionally be a transmission tunnel, allowing for a low seating position. The seats, however, are quite narrow, even for someone with an average build, and the unadjustable headrest is a bit too low. While we appreciated their copious bolstering in the corners, a wider, comfier seat would be more befitting a grand tourer.

The center console extends into the rear of the cabin, where there are two more bucket seats. While Karma claims the Gyesera has more legroom than the Revero, it hasn’t helped much. The rear seat is almost unusable for adults, with this 5-foot-11-inch writer barely able to squeeze in behind his own seating position, with his knees scrunched up and his head brushing the roof. The trunk is also quite tight, with a high floor and a fairly narrow opening.

The Gyesera is satisfying to drive for the most part. Every control has pleasing heft to it. The steering is decently communicative, and its weight builds naturally as you turn the wheel. The accelerator isn’t touchy, with the swell of power growing progressively as you press the pedal. The Gyesera weighs just over 5000 pounds and has a lengthy wheelbase, but it shrinks in the corners and feels nimble.

Although the Gyesera may not be able to match the heady power figures of other high-end electric-driven cars, it still packs plenty of verve. Launch it off the line, and the rear tires chirp before the torque-vectoring system finds traction and shoots you forward. Get too excited with the throttle coming out of a corner, and the rear end tries to break loose. It’s not terribly hard to overwhelm the Goodyear Eagle F1 tires, which measure 255/35R-22 up front and 285/35R-22 at the rear, giving the Gyesera a bit of a playful edge.

Braking is handled by Brembo 14-inch rotors, with six-piston calipers up front and four-piston calipers at the rear. The brakes are strong, although the car occasionally felt a bit skittish under heavy deceleration, and while the blending of regenerative braking and the friction brakes is decent, the pedal doesn’t give much feedback. The three levels of regenerative braking are adjusted by the right-side steering-wheel-mounted paddle. The weakest setting is very light, while the strongest setting is close to one-pedal driving but won’t bring the car to a complete stop.

The left paddle selects the drive mode: Stealth, Sustain, or Sport. In Stealth, the engine stays off and the Gyesera glides along on electric power. Sustain fires up the engine, running in its most efficient mode to maintain the battery charge level. The engine hums away in the background most of the time but occasionally gets intrusively loud.

In Sport mode, the engine works as hard as possible to replenish the battery. Sport also opens up the exhaust, but this is actually one of the Gyesera’s biggest flaws. The three-cylinder sounds, frankly, terrible, with a buzzy note and a flatulent thwack when you let off the throttle at high rpm. The engine is also constantly kicking on and off, making its rasp even more noticeable, since every time you lift, the cacophony completely falls away. The exhaust also exits right underneath the driver’s-side door, exacerbating the din. It’s a sound that’s more befitting a hot hatch than a luxury GT. The recently revealed one-off Karma Eximius 1 trades the three-cylinder for a 6.2-liter V-8, and we think a roaring V-8 would be far more fitting in the Gyesera.

The ride quality, however, helps restore the Gyesera’s upscale positioning. The car rides on Öhlins coil-over dampers and features unequal-length control arms at the front and rear. Despite not having adaptive dampers or air springs, the ride is smooth and comfortable, without feeling floaty, and the Gyesera still keeps body roll in check. It’s the ideal blend of comfort and agility, a ride that won’t punish you on rough surfaces but still provides plenty of confidence in the corners.

The Gyesera is, ultimately, a niche product, although that’s at least partially intentional. The first 50 units are set to reach dealerships before the end of this year, and the Gyesera will remain a low-production, handcrafted model. Prices start at $139,995, although the one we drove was optioned up to $158,995. That’s not cheap, and the powertrain isn’t nearly as rousing as those in high-performance sedans from Mercedes-AMG, Porsche, and BMW. But the Gyesera counters with a head-turning design, high-end materials, a well-balanced ride, and sporty handling, while also offering the feeling of instant electric torque and the ability to travel up to 80 miles without using gas. This incarnation of the slinky plug-in hybrid sedan is much improved and shows promise for the latest rebirth of Karma Automotive.

#4545. Honda just showed off its first high-end electric mountain bike

Honda makes just about everything with a motor, from lawnmowers and generators to cars, motorcycles, and even airplanes. Now the Japanese giant is adding another electrified vehicle to the list – a premium electric mountain bike.

Unveiled at EICMA 2026 in Milan, the new Honda RN0 marks the company’s first entry into the premium electric mountain bike market. And unlike many automotive-branded e-bikes that amount to little more than a licensing deal and a familiar logo slapped on someone else’s frame, Honda appears to have actually put some engineering muscle behind this one.

The RN0 was jointly developed with German high-end e-MTB manufacturer ROTWILD and features a proprietary carbon monocoque frame and distinctive gull-arm swingarm inspired by Honda’s motorcycle chassis development experience.

There’s actually some real history behind that connection. Honda experimented with mountain bike development in the early 2000s, culminating in its wild RN01 downhill racing bike. In 2005, that project won the overall series championship in the UCI Mountain Bike Downhill World Cup. Honda never turned the RN01 into a consumer bicycle, but more than two decades later, the RN0 is effectively picking up where the company previously left off.

The roughly 24 kg (53 lb) RN0 is set up as a multi-role electric mountain bike, featuring 160 mm FOX 36 FLOAT Factory Kashima front suspension paired with a FOX FLOAT X Factory Kashima rear shock. DT Swiss H1900 SPLINE wheels use a mullet setup with a 29-inch wheel up front and 27.5-inch wheel in the rear, while Shimano DEORE XT four-piston brakes handle stopping duties.

Those are some quality components, but the drivetrain may be even more interesting.

Honda is using Shimano’s new 2.3 kg drive unit, rated for up to 100 Nm of torque and 750 watts of maximum output, paired with a sizeable 720 Wh battery.

Shimano’s AUTO ASSIST can automatically vary motor assistance based on terrain and rider input, while AUTO SHIFT handles gear changes to maintain an appropriate cadence.

There’s even an Assist Carryover function that briefly continues providing power after pedaling stops, potentially making it easier to clear rocks, roots, and other technical obstacles that normally would see the assist grind to a halt right when it is needed most.

A 2.2-inch color display is integrated directly into the top tube, and there’s USB-C charging plus Shimano app connectivity for adjusting motor settings and electronically locking the bike.

Honda hasn’t yet announced pricing in its release, but with a carbon chassis, Factory-level FOX suspension, XT brakes, and premium Shimano electronics, don’t expect this to be the everyman’s electric bike.

If anything, the RN0 looks much more like Honda is finally bringing its motorcycle engineering mentality back to mountain bikes – this time with a battery and motor along for the ride.
