#4431. 10 Pokémon That Are the Biggest Red Flags

Aden Carter is a Contributor at DualShockers who has been covering games professionally since 2020. He specializes in lists and guides, with a focus on RPGs, horror games, survival horror, Soulslikes, cozy/sim games, and action-adventure titles. Before joining DualShockers, Aden contributed to GameRant, XDA, Gamepur, I

There are over 1,000 Pokémon now and they span nine generations of games. Over the years, there have been many Pokémon designs, with some of them being fantastic, and others being rather… questionable.

With that being said, everyone has a favorite Pokémon, but not all of them convey a positive or welcoming message. In fact, some of them are serious red flags to have as your favorite.

These Pokémon will make others cringe for obvious reasons, and possibly even question your taste. Sometimes it is about the Pokémon’s look, other times the Pokédex is to blame, and you can even blame society for others.

Charizard has been around since the beginning of the Pokémon series, and it quickly became a Pokémon that was beloved by everyone. Many of us were around to see Ash take in Charmander, and help it grow into a fiery beast.

However, there are many who consider Charizard to be a big red flag when choosing your favorite Pokémon. The reason for this is that you are far too basic if this is your choice.

Of course, there is a lot of context behind Charizard being a red flag. After all, it is the Pokémon that has received some of the most attention, with it getting multiple forms and promotions. It’s almost like Charizard is the mascot of Pokémon with how much attention it gets.

From the Eevee evolutions to Magikarp becoming something useful, here are the Pokémon in FireRed and LeafGreen that feel different after evolving.

The original generation of Pokémon was something that blew the minds of many kids. However, the magic that once created something that everyone loved ended up creating some rather poorly designed monsters in later generations.

One Pokémon design that felt uninspired is the Trubbish line, as it is nothing more than a bag of garbage that evolves into a pile of trash. Garbodor is nothing more than a trash pile that many associate with being smelly.

The internet ruined Garbodor by turning it into a meme where if you like the Pokémon, you are considered dirty. On the other hand, many associate this Pokémon as a red flag because choosing it feels like someone is purposefully trying to go against the grain by choosing a less universally loved Pokémon.

In past years, if you’d ask someone who their favorite Pokémon is, there was a large sect of the fan base that would say Typhlosion. He used to be cool, but everything changed when content was leaked that involved this once-innocent Pokémon.

As part of the leak in 2024, Typhlosion - specifically the Hisuian form - received some unsettling lore that involved folklore of it shapeshifting into a human and kidnapping a young girl. There’s more to it, but I don’t want to dive that deep.

Despite the leak never containing any canon information that made it into the games, and there being mistranslations, and other issues with it, Typhlosion has never really been able to escape the allegations, and so therefore, is still considered a red flag to many in the fan base.

When you bring together many people and give them the capability of being anonymous, as they can be on the internet, they have a habit of ruining everything you once loved. While there are multiple on this list, Lopunny is the first up.

Lopunny started off as Buneary - a rather adorable rabbit Pokémon - that gets an… interesting physique when it evolves into its final stage. Many saw this transformation, went online, and then proceeded to turn the Pokémon into a symbol for provocation.

Since then, it has been frowned upon whenever someone mentions that their favorite Pokémon is Lopunny, and the addition of Mega Lopunny did not help. Instead, it made things a bit worse.

Mr. Mime was an unsettling Pokémon when kids were introduced to it in the anime. Its human-like appearance mixed with a mime is something that is uncanny. However, it has only gotten worse over the years.

Digging through its Pokédex entries, you learn that it is capable of creating physical objects that are invisible. Along with that, if you interrupt its performance, it feels the need to slap you with its big flat hands.

This alone is weird, but you can add on the allegations that Mr. Mime is Ash’s stepfather in the anime. To cap it off, Mr. Mime got even more strange with the Detective Pikachu movie, further enhancing its uncanny and unsettling nature.

Did you choose Garchomp because you like the Pokémon, or did you choose it because it is a powerhouse and you are someone who gets overly competitive and sweaty during competition? Maybe it’s because you still have PTSD from Cynthia destroying you in Diamond and Pearl?

This is often what is associated with the love of Garchomp. There is no denying that Garchomp is an absolute beast of a Pokémon that can destroy others in competition, but that also makes many believe that those who like Garchomp have a far too competitive and aggressive mindset.

The other mindset people have is that Garchomp is associated with Cynthia from Diamond and Pearl. She dominated players in that era, and the idea is that those who like Garchomp haven’t gotten over that and want to inflict the same trauma on others.

There are Pokémon who have off Pokédex entries, with some of them being focused on some sort of trauma or horror story. Drifloon is one such Pokémon, with it being a ghost Pokémon who is known for kidnapping children.

The original Pokédex entries don’t make Drifloon out to be so bad, as the Dex says that it pulls on children to steal them away, but it ends up getting yanked around instead. However, this has gotten worse with time.

More recent entries specifically state that this Pokémon kidnaps children and whisks them off to the afterlife. Other entries talk about how it is specifically filled with souls and grows larger each time it steals one away. Let’s just leave this Pokémon out of our favorites list.

Pokemon Red/Blue's Lavender Town remains one of the eeriest creations in video gaming.

The internet has a way of taking any Pokémon that has slightly humanoid features and turning them into your worst nightmare. Similar to Lopunny before it, Gothitelle fell victim to those who seek to ruin things for other people.

Again, this is another Pokémon evolution line that starts off very innocent, with Gothita being a rather cute Pokémon that is very innocent in appearance. Unfortunately, that changes when it reaches its final evolution.

There is nothing innately wrong about liking this evolution line, but it definitely calls your taste into question, and many will immediately see the red flag fly, and it is completely understandable.

I am not sure that this even needs to be said because, of all the Pokémon with a humanoid appearance, Gardevoir has been treated the worst. Originally introduced in generation 3, the entire Raltz evolution line was loved, but then things went south very quickly.

Gardevoir is a Pokémon that resembles a woman in a flowing dress. Its body consists of said dress, which is more or less a flowing gown, and it has a hairstyle that appears to be done for a pageant or evening event.

However, this is enough to get the internet riled up, and Gardevoir was the first of the Pokémon of this style to be twisted by those who just seek to ruin things for other people. Now, this Pokémon is considered one of the biggest red flags of the franchise.

Eevee was, and still is, one of the most popular Pokémon there is, with many finding the little fox-like creature to be adorable. When it was introduced, it was beloved, and so were its original three evolutions; Flareon, Jolteon, and Vaporeon.

Unfortunately for Vaporeon, it became the fascination of one of the most perverse corners of the Pokémon fan base. So much so that it was treated far worse than Lopunny, Gothitelle, and Gardivoire combined.

The information about this Pokémon soon became a meme that spread like wildfire, leading to many victims being caught in the smoke. Now, many are ashamed to even talk about Vaporeon in a positive light, as it looks bad. What was once one of the most famous Pokémon of a generation has now become the biggest red flag in the fandom.

While most pokemon are friendly and nice, some are much more mischievous and ready to cause harm. Here are Pokemon ready to rob you in broad daylight

#4429. Arc Raiders patch nerfs the Deadline mine, ends the menace of the Venator

The first post-Stella Montis patch for Arc Raiders has arrived, and it predictably touches much of what people brought to the latest map.

Arc Raiders has received a new update today that’s almost entirely dedicated to balance and economy tweaks. Patch 1.3.0 arrived earlier across all platforms, coming in at just under 1GB. This is an especially interesting patch because many of the changes it makes can be seen as a response to player behaviour on Stella Montis, the game’s latest map, which just joined the roster last week.

Stella Montis is available for players who’ve put in a decent number of rounds, and its close-quarters, enclosed environments have essentially turned it into the new “PvP map”, where constant action can be found.

That, of course, also means that the map has exposed a few balance issues with some of the game’s weapons and tools. Case in point: the Venator, a pistol that saw a lot of use recently. The weapon is especially powerful when fully-upgraded, something Arc Raiders developer Embark said pushed it beyond what had been originally intended.

In today’s update, the Venator's fire rate is the thing getting hit the hardest, with each upgrade now offering slower gains to the weapon's rate-of-fire compared to the way things were. The weapon’s weight is also being increased to five from two.

Another powerful item players have been getting a lot of mileage out of recently has been the Deadline mine. Unlike the Venator, the Deadline is mainly a threat to Arc enemies, and it’s proven incredibly powerful against the largest and most fearsome, such as the Bastion, and Leaper. In fact, the mine was considered essential when taking down a Queen.

The patch vastly increases its purchase price, and makes it more difficult to craft by upping the amount each of its components requires. Perhaps the most effective nerf, however, is the reduction to the Deadline’s stock at traders from three to just one, which means you’re going to be seeing a lot less of it topside.

Beyond those specific changes, Embark has also tweaked explosive damage across the board. According to the developer, explosive damage was being applied to multiple parts at once, which trivialised some encounters.

This change mainly affects larger Arc units, such as the Bastion, allowing them to withstand more explosive damage before bits start coming off of them. The Hullcracker, one of the best explosive damage weapons, has also caught a nerf as part of that.

Check the official blog for the full change log for patch 1.3.0. If you’re just getting started with the hottest extraction shooter ever, our Arc Raiders tips offer plenty of help. You should also learn what all the different Map Conditions do in Arc Raiders, and how to best make use of each of them.

Battlefield 6 sales are setting all kinds of records, but one in particular has long eluded the Battlefield series.

If you’ve been paying any attention to the shooter market these past few months, you won’t be surprised to learn that Battlefield 6 has been an unprecedented success for EA, and the Battlefield series as a whole.

The game managed to sell over 7 million units at launch, climbing to the top of the charts anywhere you look, including setting new series concurrent player records on Steam. Thanks to new data, we now better understand the true scale of this launch.

The latest Circana report, which looks at game and hardware sales in the United States, has arrived. This iteration covers the month of October, which is when Battlefield 6 was released.

Battlefield 6 was the top-selling game across all platforms during October - which isn’t surprising. It has overtaken NBA 2K26 to become 2025’s best-selling game year-to-date, making it the best-selling Battlefield game ever.

In October alone, the game sold more than the lifetime sales of Battlefield 1, previously the best-selling entry in the franchise.

Battlefield 6 even set records beyond just its own series, having now produced the highest single-month dollar sales (physical and digital) total for any full game released in the last three years. The previous record holder was 2022’s Modern Warfare 2.

November’s report, which is set to arrive midway through December, will show, once and for all, whether Battlefield 6 has been able to overtake Black Ops 7. With one exception, Call of Duty games have, for more than a decade, topped the best-selling year-to-date chart. Regardless of the quality of the individual titles, or the competition in any given year, nothing has been able to shake that dominance.

Given all this momentum, Battlefield 6 has a shot at dethroning Call of Duty this year, beating Black Ops 7 to become the year’s best-seller. You never want to count out the sheer popularity of Call of Duty among casual players, however, which is what’s going to make December’s report all the more interesting.

#4425. PUBG's extraction shooter spin-off, Black Budget, is finally going to be playable next month

The most interesting development in the PUBG universe, PUBG: Black Budget, is almost ready to show itself off to a wider group of players.

You’d be forgiven for not remembering PUBG: Black Budget, the extraction off-shoot of the original battle royale shooter, PUBG. Black Budget has been sort of floating around the internet for months, but Krafton never really committed to revealing core details about the game, or when players will actually get to play it.

This changes today, as the publisher - along with the game’s developer, PUBG Studios, have finally lifted the lid off the upcoming shooter.

Black Budget is described as a “tactical” extraction shooter. Squads of players infiltrate a mysterious island trapped in a time loop. There’s a bit of a STALKER element here with anomalies and various, unpredictable environmental shifts.

Coli, the island in question, hides a research facility that holds secrets and artefacts, which is what players will be attempting to extract. This is very much a PvPvE shooter, though PUBG Studios says the focus will be on exploration and discovery, rather than constant combat.

The game’s first set of closed alpha tests is set for December. The first takes place December 12-14, and another is scheduled for December 19-21. That’s six days across two weeks, with the test only being available on PC. Both sessions will be open to players in North America, Europe, and Asia.

As it usually works with these sorts of tets on Steam, the game’s Steam page has a link where you can request access. If granted, you’ll be able to find the closed alpha in your library and download it when the time comes.

Though this is a closed test, Krafton confirmed that players will be able to capture and livestream their gameplay. In fact, watching content creators might be how you get access, as Black Budget is going to have a Twitch Drops event running alongside those sessions.

When I played Arc Raiders prior to its launch, I likened its tense and uncertain atmosphere to that of the early days of PUBG, so it’s going to be very interesting to see what actual PUBG does with the extraction shooter premise.

So far, it sounds like it’s going to be doing its own thing, leaning more into the adventure side of the subgenre, but we’ll have to see how it all shakes out when the tests start. Indeed, the BR-like constantly shrinking circle sounds like it could be a game-changing twist.

The Moon-Prayer Night is the big in-world festival, marking Dameselette's final night before she sets off for the moon. The new update, of course, introduces new playable characters, one with an interesting mechanic.

The events of this new chapter take place following Rarcher of Solnari’s defeat. The victory has given way to the Moon-Prayer Night celebrations, which brings various stalls to the Nasha Town, alongside a new souvenir stamp book where you can record your memories.

All is not fine, however, as Alice and Nicole Reeyn come bearing some bad news about phantoms appearing across the Nod-Krai region at Teyvat's borders. There’s a mystery to be uncovered here, and your journey to do so won’t be a lonely one.

This is how you can earn the 4-Star Rainbow Serpent's Rain Bow, too.

Beyond that, you can also look forward to the Miliastra Wonderland UGC module getting new updates. The Wonderland Resource Center is where creators can get and share resources through the editing tool.

#4422. 2027 Chevrolet Silverado HD, a Gorilla-Strong Pickup You Don’t Have to Wrestle With

A monstrously torquey new 8.3-liter turbo-diesel V-8 and new electric power steering make this heavy-duty pickup easy to drive.

The lightest Atlas stone used in international strongman competitions is 220 pounds. The heaviest is nearly 500 pounds. Extremely large, frighteningly strong people lift these big orbs onto shoulder-high plinths, and just watching it will give you an inferiority complex—and sciatica. Luckily, there’s a way to feel a similar sense of broad-shouldered accomplishment without spending a lifetime in the gym. Drive the 2027 Chevy Silverado Heavy-Duty (HD) pickup, preferably with a trailer attached, and you’ll get the same rush of endorphins as 2026 World Strongest Man champion Mitchell Hooper as he lifted spheres and repped deadlifts of over 800 pounds.

While the 2027 Silverado 1500 got a full redesign for 2027, the HD is mostly carryover in body and interior. Still, it has some new delights, the biggest and most delightful being the new 8.3-liter Duramax V-8 turbo-diesel engine. This big brute belts out 555 horsepower and 1230 pound-feet of torque, is backed by a 10-speed automatic transmission, and makes light work of towing even the heaviest trailer.

See all results for new 2027 Chevrolet Silverado 2500HD / 3500HD for sale near 95131

To keep the burly engine happy, the HD trucks have a revised cooling system with a four-deep stack of radiators, charge coolers, and oil coolers. To keep the driver cool when stopping a fully loaded HD pickup, 14.6-inch front brake rotors clamped by four-piston calipers replace the outgoing model’s two-piston binders. An electronic brake booster, a first for a heavy-duty pickup, gives the brake pedal a similar feel to what you’d find in a regular SUV, no heavy foot needed for effective braking.

To demonstrate the diesel’s grunt, Chevy hooked up a massive trailer loaded with construction equipment and let us rip, towing nearly 37,000 pounds down a drag strip. The new trucks are rated for up to 38,000 pounds with a gooseneck trailer (when equipped with the Max Trailering package). The NHRA won’t be adding a sled-pulling class to its competition anytime soon, but the big truck moved out with barely a shudder, and the upgraded brakes and e-booster made stopping at the far end as easy as launching. The most intimidating part of the pull was making the turnout at the end of the strip, but the HD’s smooth power delivery and redesigned steering made for a drama-free turn despite the tight corner.

The 2500 HD lineup encompasses six trims, starting with the WT (Work Truck) and topping out with the optioned-up High Country. The base engine remains a 6.6-liter gas-burning V-8 (distinct from the similarly sized optional V-8 in redesigned 2027 light-duty models), albeit updated to now develop 412 horsepower and 472 pound-feet of torque. The new Duramax V-8 is an $11,400 option, and it’s available on all trims. That’s a big jump from the outgoing 6.6-liter diesel V-8, which added only $9990 to the HD’s price. Luckily for truck shoppers, overall starting prices see a smaller price hike. The MSRP for the 2027 WT begins at $49,995 (an increase of $1000 versus 2026), and the High Country now starts at $78,195.

See all results for new 2027 Chevrolet Silverado 2500HD / 3500HD for sale near 95131

Step up into the cabin—or haul yourself up with the grab handle—and you’ll find the interior is little changed from 2026 models. It’s spacious and cushy with big storage compartments, but the design and the dash layout are the same as before. What is new is some of the software available through the 13.4-inch center touchscreen. There’s an updated Tow/Haul mode that fine-tunes power delivery, shift points, and braking to make for smoother towing up and downhill. An Off-Road mode allows more wheelspin to prevent bog-downs, and off-road-oriented ZR2 HDs get the same Terrain mode as the light-duty version, a trail-focused tune that teams the throttle with automatic braking for what’s essentially one-pedal driving during off-roading. Optional camera add-ons make for up to 14 different views, including an invisible-trailer mode and a split screen when reversing. In the various camera views, the HD lacks the light duty’s helpful graphic overlays, but it’s probably fair to assume that buyers of heavy-duty trucks aren’t beginners at towing.

Another feature that has not made its way from light duty to heavy duty is Chevy’s Super Cruise hands-free driving. In the past, this was because the HD still used a hydraulic steering system, but a major change for 2027 is the switch to electric power steering. The new rack-and-pinion electric steering setup is another first for the HD, and it makes a big difference in the feedback through the wheel and consistency of steering feel even during braking and hard steering inputs. It gives the HD a more consumer-friendly feel. On a mountain road, these big rigs feel manageable, and while you still won’t want to swing a tight U-turn, there’s no fighting the wheel when changing direction. While this year’s trucks won’t offer Super Cruise, the technology is in place for GM to fit additional driver aids in the future.

That omission aside, the theme of the HDs’ changes for 2027 is ease of use. Most of what’s new isn’t visible from the outside, but it’s all designed to make the tasks of hauling and towing feel less like a job and more like a cruise in a passenger vehicle—a really burly passenger vehicle.

#4421. Battlefield 6 kicks off its first free trial post the Black Ops 7 launch to twist that knife

Activision has done its own fair share of Battlefield 6 counterprogramming prior to that game's release, and EA is here to repay the favour with Black Ops 7.

Even if you don’t care about the rivalries between the top multiplayer first-person shooters series, it’s hard to ignore how much EA wanted to stick it to Call of Duty this year with Battlefield 6.

Activision saw that coming early enough that it ran multiple free weekends around major moments for EA’s game, including its launch, seemingly in an effort to capture some of those players and keep them away from BF6.

Both Battlefield 6, and Black Ops 7 have now launched, and though exact sales figures may never be detrmined (though EA did announce 7 million sold in the first week), it’s very clear at this point from every metric we can see that BF6 came out on top this year.

The recent Black Ops 7 launch clearly hasn’t made many people happy, so just like Activision made Black Ops 6 free to play at BF6’s launch, EA has now done the same with its own game. The Battlefield 6 free trial, which was announced last week, is just an hour away at the time of this writing.

This is the first trial for the core game, and it arrives some six weeks after Battlefield 6 officialy launched, and four weeks following the release of the free-to-play Battlefield Redsec, which has battle royale and other components.

Beyond all the drama surrounding the two rival shooter franchises, the Battlefield 6 trial is itself pretty straightfoward, and is notably nowhere near as genrous as some of the Call of Duty ones we’ve seen recently.

The trial goes live today at 4am PT, 7am ET, 12pm GMT across all platforms, and will be available for a week; ending Tuesday, December 2. It includes three core maps: Siege of Cairo, Eastwood, and Blackwell Fields.

Players will have access to four game modes, played on different versions of the same maps. Conquest, Breakthrough, Sabotage, and Team Deathmatch will all be available to choose from, and there don’t appear to be any level or XP limits in the trial.

Unfortunatley, just as the free trial was about to go live, the game got hit with a major matchmaking outage that took down all matchmaking in the core game, leaving Redsec unaffected.

Hopefully EA can resolve this issue before the trial officially kicks off.

#4420. 10 Soulslikes That Are Unexpected Masterpieces

Ronald is a video game journalist with more than 10 years of experience in the industry, working on several of the most important Spanish websites.

Creating a new genre is quite difficult, and while that's not exactly what FromSoftware did, it certainly gave rise to a new generation of titles aptly categorized under the Soulslike label.

The reasons why this phenomenon emerged organically and without premeditation are plentiful, as are the numerous gems that its rise to popularity among developers has gifted us.

Gradually, the niche became a popular segment among creators and players, but even so, its expansion has been such that many creations, despite their quality, have flown under the radar of most.

Therefore, in order to give due recognition to those works that oscillate between being unknown and not properly appreciated, I invite you to read this list of ten Soulslikes that are unexpected masterpieces.

As a self-proclaimed devotee of boss rushes, especially given that they're always the most interesting aspect of any Soulslike, no amount of praise is enough to highlight Rubinite's current popularity.

Despite its branching nature, it features an engaging story that perfectly complements the gameplay, which isn't the sole focus of the title; rather, both elements work together to create a truly well-rounded experience.

However, it's clear that anyone playing Rubinite will do so for the bosses (or for its gorgeous pixel art), and in this department, it performs sensationally, with varied adversaries in both aesthetics and gimmicks that truly maximize the game's satisfying mechanics.

As one of the year's best indie games, it inevitably makes the list of the most outstanding Soulslikes, especially since it pleasantly surprised me even though I'd been eagerly awaiting its release since the day it was announced.

The so-called flow state is a subtle key to the excellence of a Soulslike, as the magnificent AI LIMIT demonstrates through its simple yet direct combat that truly manages to captivate you from the first touch.

I admit I'm usually wary of titles that share its visual style due to past bad experiences, though this game reversed my expectations with its solid gameplay, both in its design and execution.

AI LIMIT's game feel is the experience's highlight, with mesmerizing encounters that, while not at the most challenging end, strike a perfect balance between being challenging and never frustrating.

If your mind, like mine, unconsciously compares it to similar products within and outside Soulslikes, I recommend you completely dispel any doubts, as few other examples of the genre can offer this level of reward.

If you remember the feeling you had the first time you played a Soulsborne game, that pleasant wonder of being captivated as you discovered an expansive world brimming with majesty, then encountering Mohrta is a gift from heaven.

Despite the obvious gameplay differences, since the game is both an FPS and an ARPG, the sense of discovery is practically the same, generating indescribable joy when you come across a new weapon, enemy, area, or NPC.

Everything in the game is so bizarre yet charming that it's difficult to play it in short bursts, because what it really makes you want to do is burn the midnight oil while enjoying its unparalleled inventiveness in terms of story, worldbuilding, and design.

If you've played any other title from its developer, Scumhead, you can more or less imagine what Mohrta has in store, though I can already tell you that it's the best video game this eccentric creator has ever produced.

There's nothing more fitting for this season than being destroyed by the same boss fifty-seven times in a row.

While I always found Mortal Shell a fascinating exercise in imagination within a dark and obtuse fantasy setting, I always considered it merely good, nothing more, but I can't say the same for Mortal Shell II.

Coming from a first title that was rough around the edges and failed to fully convince, Cold Symmetry surpassed even the most optimistic predictions with a sequel that addresses its predecessor's every single flaw.

The enemies' legibility, ease of spatial awareness, combat's feel, orientation within the main content, level design's firmness... It's comparatively much more robust, and I'd be lying if I said I expected such a significant leap in quality.

Therefore, Mortal Shell II proved me wrong, and nothing could make me happier. That it belongs in the discussion of the best Soulslikes of all time is undeniable at this point, yet it doesn't rank higher on the list because I'm sure there were devotees who knew this would be the outcome.

Bloodborne is the kind of video game that, once you finish it, leaves you with the bittersweet feeling that you'll never experience anything like it again, but Vigil: The Longest Night comes pretty close.

Although its gameplay is much more tactical and careful than its 3D counterpart, its atmosphere is undeniably analogous, especially due to the artistic and narrative similarities that place both within the realm of cosmic and body horror.

From there on, the comparisons begin to diminish, as it's more reminiscent of Salt and Sanctuary in its combat and progression systems, though its founding elements are masterfully aligned with FromSoftware's prodigious child.

Therefore, Vigil: The Longest Night achieves a feat that very few others can: making you feel like you're playing Bloodborne. This might seem like a weak argument for calling it a masterpiece, but when you truly grasp the difficulty of such an undertaking, it's not so far-fetched after all.

If you haven't played Queen's Domain yet, be sure to leave this article open in another tab while you download it, because one of the most immersive games of 2026 awaits you.

If King's Field were released today, I'm sure it would strive to resemble the work of Freshly Baked Games LLC, whom I was honored to discover through their debut title, The New Flesh, and with whom I've been inseparable ever since.

The decision to follow their lead was the right one, as keeping an eye out for the release of their retro-fantasy action RPG has given me one of the year's finest experiences, especially since I love titles inspired by Dark Souls more for their level design, interconnectivity, and progression than for their combat systems.

Some might say that Queen's Domain isn't Soulslike enough because it aligns more with the philosophy than the practicalities, but for me, that's enough, as it's one of the most highly recommended and captivating games released in the last couple of months.

In these Soulslikes, studying your enemy and playing carefully is vital.

Soulslikes tend to be very traditional in terms of what they do and how they do it, but the arrival of an outsider to the genre like One More Level brought a breath of fresh air in the form of Valor Mortis.

As the creators of Ghostrunner, a first-person platformer that excels in its spectacular movement sequences, their ARPG inherited that skill to create the most enjoyable experience in the genre in terms of movement.

The levels are gigantic in scale and verticality, allowing you to fly through the air using a grappling hook, run along walls, and swing to ledges, giving it a completely unique feel that no other Soulslike has ever achieved.

Add to that combat that balances parries and dodges like Lies of P, spectacular and grotesque (though easy) bosses, and customization options that are limited but refined, and you realize that Valor Mortis is much more than what people say about it.

Considering they had just released the least-reviewed Darksiders game to date, nobody bet a penny on Gunfire Games' success with Remnant: From the Ashes, and yet nobody remained silent when it came to praising its remarkable quality.

Making a permanently cooperative title with third-person shooter mechanics in a sporadically online and predominantly melee branch is among the boldest moves the genre has ever seen, which is already quite an achievement.

Regardless, Remnant: From the Ashes doesn't stand out simply for its innovation; it's a robust and extremely fun game whose variety of weapons, bosses, and environments allows for a deep adventure, brimming with content that's worth experiencing in its entirety.

Its breakout performance is a bit of a blow to me, as I suspect that, over the years, they'll prioritize this IP over Darksiders, but if that's the sacrifice to keep getting the best co-op games in the genre... so be it.

The First Berserker: Khazan's announcement certainly didn't leave any avid fan indifferent, as it gave the impression of being a major beast within the genre, but I don't think anyone could have anticipated its true severity.

Although its average critical reception is more mixed, I'm more inclined to agree with the unanimous opinion of the gaming community that it's a serious contender to be FromSoftware's ultimate heir.

It's difficult to describe what you have to feel to comprehend it truly, but holding the controls while fighting The First Berserker: Khazan's bosses is an untamed magic that courses through your entire body, filling you with adrenaline and excitement that are tough to match.

Were it not for the somewhat simplistic nature of its basic enemies and environments, the discussion about the title would be very different, yet you forget all of that when you enter the zone of maximum concentration thanks to its diverse, refined, and satisfying gameplay.

Every genre has its defining features, and the Soulslike is one that gets misunderstood fairly often with games like these blurring the line.

The only reason I disagree with those who believe the previous Soulslike is the best of them all is due to Lies of P's existence, a title that no one even came close to predicting, even if today it is commonly recognized under said distinction.

When we talk about unexpected masterpieces, the fact that NEOWIZ, a company originally conceived to distribute music games for the PlayStation Portable, developed the only Soulslike capable of rivaling the originals is among the entire century's most unpredictable events.

No matter how much faith you had in its release, there was no way to imagine that Lies of P would have such a vast arsenal, iconic and demandingly engaging bosses, levels crafted to perfection, a spectacular soundtrack, and even a story that keeps you engaged until the very last second.

Add to that its worldbuilding, side quests, flawless combination of parries and dodges, level of customization through the weapon assembly system, masterful enemy positioning and shortcuts... and you're left with a title that can only be described as majestic.

Lies of P raised the bar for the genre to a new level, and since 2024, it has become the ultimate benchmark despite coming from such a modest and distant background as that of its creators.

Dispatch, a superhero-themed workplace comedy from last year, celebrates its one-year anniversary today. While it was released episodically, the first batch dropped on October 22. Today, developer AdHoc announced a batch of anniversary content, and some of it drops today.

First, there's a new way to play Dispatch: storyboard mode. This option lets you play through the whole experience using the original animatics – rough placeholder sketches that the artists used to sync images up to the voice-over. It's a fun behind-the-scenes look at the game's development that we don't get very often. In that same vein, the cast and crew recorded DVD-style commentary tracks to play over the game, making jokes and sharing insight into the development process. A press release says there are over 16 hours of commentary from the game's development team (like art director Derek Stratton and creative directors Dennis Lenart and Nick Herman) as well as some of the cast, including Aaron Paul, Laura Bailey, and Erin Yvette.

Storyboard and Commentary modes are included in the game's deluxe edition, which you can upgrade to for $10.99. Both modes are available today.

If you haven't played the game yet, AdHoc has announced a new way to do so; Dispatch is coming to mobile platforms on December 9. It's been rebuilt to support touch controls and vertical play, and it will be available on iOS and Android. You can even play the first half of the game for free – the first four episodes are included, but you'll need to pay $19.99 to play the rest.

Finally, AdHoc announced new merch, including a book created alongside publisher Lost in Cult called Dispatch: Design Works, which is both an art book and a "making-of" book. There's also a live game soundtrack concert in Los Angeles featuring Thot Squad, Bershy, Primer, Caroline Kingsbury, Fartbarf, and Dispatch composer Andrew Arcadi with the SDN Company Band. It will be held at Avalon Hollywood on December 3, but it won't be livestreamed, so you'll need to grab a ticket to see the event. The press release states that people who signed up for updates from adhocstudio.com will be the first in line to purchase tickets.

#4416. Tenebris Somnia Review – A Hair-Raising And Entertaining Throwback

Tenebris Somnia channels the old-school appeal of classic point-and-click adventures, survival horror, and full-motion-video (FMV) experiences, then smartly modernizes them to create a creepy, entertaining experience. Surviving the twisted threats of a demonic dream world is a tightly packed adventure that rewards you with what’s essentially an impressive indie horror film peppered throughout. It’s a nightmare you may not want to wake up from.

The blend of live-action and in-game storytelling works well in Tenebris Somina’s adventure, which begins when protagonist Julia visits the apartment of her filmmaker ex-boyfriend, Ivan, after suffering recurring nightmares of him being massacred by monsters. What begins as a well-meaning check-in on his status spirals down an unsettling rabbit hole when Julia’s worst fears are realized and then some. The dialogue-free tale presents a scary but fascinating exploration of obsession, both in art and in romance, that constantly delivers surprising, and at times upsetting, revelations during its eight-hour runtime. While Tenebris Somnia sometimes leans a little too far into “tell, don’t show” territory when explaining the cool lore of its supernatural threats, I never felt lost or confused about the wild things that regularly unfold on screen.

FMV experiences are nothing new, but Tenebris Somnia’s live-action scenes are a highlight. They’re well shot, sport impressively gruesome practical effects, and even present visual clues that make them important to gameplay. These scenes are additive, never taking too much time away from the in-game action, and they feel well placed to elicit the strongest emotional response. I also appreciate how the live scenes fit thematically, as much of Tenebris Somnia’s tale centers on a horror film shot by Ivan and Julia that significantly impacted their former relationship; at times, it’s like watching a movie about the movie. While I enjoy smaller moments, like opening a door to trigger a live-action jump scare, the filmmaking succeeds in selling Julia's emotions and the cast's reactions. Seeing real fear, concern, and determination in Julia’s eyes as she navigates a dreamworld made up of Ivan’s memories helped endear me to what would otherwise be a featureless pixel sprite.

Gameplay may look unimpressive due to its old-school adventure game presentation, but Tenebris Somnia’s spin on familiar survival-horror mechanics hits the right notes. Taking place entirely within a dreamlike version of a four-story apartment building, you’ll traverse floors collecting and combining objects and deciphering clues to solve well-crafted puzzles. I’m impressed by how well the game’s puzzles make the most of its limited graphical presentation, including clever scenarios involving mirror/screen reflections I won’t spoil, and how consistently creative they are. One devious exercise even utilizes the game’s limited save points as an unexpected resource in a way that changes how you approach your adventure going forward. No matter how strange puzzles become, they are never opaque, requiring just enough out-of-the-box thinking to make me feel smart when I connect the dots.

Battling grotesque monsters (which, naturally, look even creepier in live-action) also feels good, with melee and gunplay sporting deliberate animations reminiscent of classic adventure games without feeling mechanically clunky. Taking on multiple enemies by swinging a pipe or blowing them away with a shotgun feels better than it looks, and the most intense encounters end just as they approach the line of becoming overwhelming.

Boss battles, perhaps most unexpectedly for a largely puzzle-focused adventure, are fun and distinct from each other, be it wave-based bouts against small gremlin-like foes, protecting a fragile effigy of yourself from a parade of demented house servants, or battling literal mirror images of a tentacled flesh monster the Resident Evil series would be proud to claim. Managing limited ammo and health strikes a good balance of feeling tense but not oppressive. Playing conservatively is rewarding, as few non-boss threats need to be engaged if you can evade them well enough. But when I did find myself down to my last bullet or on the verge of death, Tenebris Somnia lets you feel the pinch just long enough before dropping a box of bullets or a health vial at the right moment.

Tenebris Somnia mines the enjoyable nostalgia of playing the horror games of yesteryear without feeling dated in the worst way. Weaving a solid indie horror film adds to the experience rather than feeling like a gimmick. The result is a captivating, well-executed survival-horror romp that maintains a hair-raising atmosphere with a fraction of the pixels of other genre giants.

But players have also been using similar exploits to clip through walls and access areas outside the playspace, allowing them to ambush enemy players and set up traps that would be impossible for others to detect.

While on the subject of being in places where you’re not supposed to, the patch blocked exterior access to the locked room inside Spaceport's Control Tower, making it only accessible from inside the tower.

#4414. NASA’s Voyager 1 is about to reach a historic one-light-day milestone

Nearly 50 years after leaving Earth, NASA's Voyager 1 is approaching an extraordinary milestone that will highlight just how far humanity's most distant spacecraft has traveled. But keeping the aging explorer operational has become an increasingly difficult challenge as its power supply slowly fades.

NASA engineers recently achieved two important developments in their effort to extend the mission. In September, they completed a complex energy conservation project designed to preserve the spacecraft's remaining scientific capabilities. Then, on October 20, Voyager 1 unexpectedly resumed communication with Earth after a mysterious 48-hour interruption.

NASA Engineers Find a Clever Way to Save Power

In early September, the Voyager team successfully replaced three devices aboard Voyager 1 with alternatives that consume less electricity. The carefully coordinated operation, nicknamed the "Big Bang," took months to prepare and was completed approximately six weeks after engineers carried out an identical procedure on Voyager 2.

The upgrade is expected to extend the operating lives of Voyager 1's remaining scientific instruments, allowing the spacecraft to continue collecting valuable information from interstellar space longer than previously expected.

Both Voyager spacecraft generate electricity using radioisotope thermoelectric generators. These systems produce electrical power from the heat released as plutonium undergoes radioactive decay. As that process continues, the spacecraft gradually lose generating capacity, with each probe experiencing a decline of approximately 4 watts annually.

After almost five decades in space, that steady loss has left engineers with very little power to spare. To keep the missions operating, NASA has progressively shut down equipment that is no longer essential.

The Big Bang presented an especially difficult engineering challenge because all three replacements had to happen simultaneously. The six devices involved help maintain temperatures inside the spacecraft despite the extreme cold of space. Replacing the three original devices together was necessary to reduce electricity consumption while preserving the proper distribution of heat throughout Voyager 1.

Keeping Voyager 1's Science Mission Alive

Power limitations have already forced NASA to deactivate two of Voyager 1's scientific instruments in recent years. When the spacecraft launched in 1977, it carried 10 instruments dedicated to scientific research. Several were shut down after Voyager completed its encounters with the outer planets, while others remained active to investigate increasingly distant regions of space.

Among the areas studied was the outer heliosphere, the enormous region of particles and magnetic fields produced by the Sun. Both Voyager spacecraft have since crossed beyond this boundary into interstellar space, making them the only spacecraft ever to directly examine the environment outside the Sun's heliosphere.

Preserving their remaining instruments is particularly important because no other missions can currently collect measurements from this distant region. Without the Big Bang upgrade, NASA would have faced the possibility of shutting down another Voyager 1 instrument as early as summer 2027.

Mysterious Communication Loss Raises New Questions

Even with the successful power conservation effort, Voyager 1 continues to encounter unexpected problems.

NASA temporarily lost contact with the spacecraft on October 18 and 19, when the agency's Deep Space Network failed to receive its radio signal during two scheduled communication attempts separated by 24 hours.

The network consists of large radio antennas at three locations around the world, allowing NASA to exchange signals with spacecraft exploring the Moon and more distant destinations. At the time of the interruption, Voyager 1 was approximately 16 billion miles (24 billion kilometers) from Earth.

After two unsuccessful attempts to detect the spacecraft, its signal unexpectedly returned on October 20, roughly 48 hours after the interruption began. Communication has remained established since then, and engineers subsequently sent commands to investigate the problem.

NASA has not yet determined exactly what caused the incident. However, engineers discovered that one set of Voyager 1's thrusters had stopped operating and that the spacecraft had automatically activated its backup thrusters.

This behavior is part of a built-in safety system known as fault protection. When the onboard computers recognize a potential problem with active equipment, they can switch to backup hardware, place the spacecraft into a stable configuration, and suspend normal activities. This gives controllers on Earth an opportunity to investigate and determine the appropriate response.

"This is the first time we've seen the spacecraft do something like this, but we are also at a point in the mission where we have to expect the unexpected," said Kareem Badaruddin, Voyager mission manager at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. "We're relieved to be back in contact with Voyager 1 and are eager to understand what happened."

Voyager 1 Approaches a Historic One-Light-Day Milestone

While NASA continues investigating the communication interruption, Voyager 1 is moving toward another remarkable achievement.

Traveling through interstellar space at approximately 38,000 mph (61,155 kph), the spacecraft is expected to reach a distance of 16.09 billion miles (25.89 billion kilometers) from Earth on November 18. That distance equals one light-day, meaning it takes light an entire 24 hours to travel between Earth and the probe.

No other human-made object has ever reached such a distance.

The milestone also illustrates the extraordinary challenges of communicating with a spacecraft so far from home. Radio waves travel at the speed of light, so commands transmitted from Earth will require a full day to reach Voyager 1. Any response sent back will take another 24 hours, creating a total communication delay of 48 hours.

"If you want to say 'hello' to Voyager, you send your message and then you go home and you wait two days before you finally get a response," said Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager at JPL.

Crossing the one-light-day threshold will not produce any physical change in Voyager 1 or its surroundings. The spacecraft will continue traveling through the same interstellar environment, unaware that it has passed a milestone of special significance to people on Earth.

Instead, the achievement serves as a powerful reminder of the enormous distances separating objects in the universe and the remarkable endurance of a spacecraft launched nearly half a century ago. Despite fading power, aging equipment, and unexpected technical problems, Voyager 1 continues its historic journey farther from Earth than any other human-made object.

The studio behind Mass Effect, Dragon Age, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, and more, has been shut down, and its last remaining project was canceled. The game in question was a fifth entry in the Mass Effect universe, and BioWare shared very little about it – not even an official name. Following the studio's closure, however, a trailer for the sci-fi sequel started circulating around the internet.

While no official BioWare representatives have confirmed that the footage is real, Bloomberg reporter Jason Schreier claims that it is. Schreier has a history of credible reporting in the field, and was the first to break the news about the layoffs. IGN has also stated that it confirmed the trailer's legitimacy.

If you want to see for yourself, you can watch the trailer on Reddit.

"The following is in-engine footage form our small team," text at the start of the video reads. "It uses our pre-production assets." The footage shows no gameplay, but includes a good-looking CG cutscene of a new protagonist speaking with an asari woman in a crowded bar. As he tells her about his life, we see glimpses of him as a soldier, then as some kind of spy, traveling to several planets to track down conflicts and "stopping them before they start." After the asari woman reveals that she's been "starting the fires" he's trying to prevent, another woman behind her lowers a hood. This new woman reveals herself as Liara T'Soni, one of Mass Effect's most iconic characters.

Then, Liara and the protagonist team up to take out the woman at the bar and her henchmen, using guns and telekinetic abilities. The trailer fades to black, then fades back in to reveal the game's would-be title: Mass Effect Universe. It's a great-looking trailer – it's a shame the game will never see the light of day.

#4410. A clever molecular trick unlocks previously impossible properties in glass

Scientists have developed a new way to change the internal structure of glass while it is being made, giving them greater control over properties such as magnetism and the way the material interacts with light. The discovery could open the door to advanced glasses with capabilities that were previously difficult or impossible to achieve.

The breakthrough comes from a collaboration involving TU Dortmund University, Paderborn University, the University of Duisburg-Essen, and the University of Oxford. Published in Nature Materials, the research demonstrates how adding a particular organic molecule during the melting process can rearrange chemical bonds within certain types of glass.

The method also allows these materials to melt at much lower temperatures, preventing the damage that would otherwise occur during manufacturing. Such specialized glasses have potential applications in gas storage, batteries, optical technologies, and catalysis.

A Molecular Trick That Changes Glass From Within

"We have found a way to chemically modify the structure of glasses derived from so-called metal-organic framework compounds - or MOFs for short - right during the manufacturing process," explains Prof. Dr. Sebastian Henke from TU Dortmund University, who led the study.

The key ingredient is a molecule called 1,10-phenanthroline. When introduced during production, it performs two important tasks. It reduces the temperature needed to melt the material while also changing how metal atoms connect with surrounding molecules.

This combination allows researchers to create glass with magnetic or light-emitting characteristics that previously could not be achieved without exposing the material to potentially destructive temperatures.

To understand why this approach matters, it helps to consider how glass normally forms. When a liquid cools quickly enough, its atoms become locked into a disordered arrangement rather than forming the repeating pattern found in crystals.

"Normally, glass is formed when a molten liquid cools rapidly. The solid structure then sets without the atoms arranging themselves in a regular pattern. Until now, researchers often had to accept the chemistry of these glasses as dictated by the starting material," explains Prof. Henke.

The new findings show that scientists can exert much greater control over this process.

Metal-organic frameworks are materials built from metal centers connected by organic compounds. By introducing phenanthroline while these materials are molten, researchers can change the chemical connections within the structure before the glass solidifies.

"The crucial point is that the molecule does not simply remain as a filler," Prof. Henke continues. "It enters into a reaction. So we are altering the chemistry at precisely the moment when the material is still liquid."

The researchers added phenanthroline to their starting materials before heating them. Once the mixture begins to melt, the molecule does more than simply lower the temperature required for melting. It actively participates in chemical reactions that reorganize the glass network.

The process changes the immediate surroundings of metal atoms by modifying their connections to neighboring molecules.

"As a flux, the substance lowers the temperature at which the material melts; as a chemical agent, the molecule binds directly to the metal atoms and partially displaces old bonds. In the molten state, the molecule interferes with what is known as the coordination environment. This term describes how many neighbors surround a single atom. Because the new molecule binds more strongly to the metal centers, the number of neighbors increases," explains Prof. Henke.

These interactions trigger a substantial rearrangement of the internal glass structure. Importantly, the researchers can control how extensively the material changes simply by adjusting the amount of phenanthroline added.

This gives scientists a practical way to tune the properties of glass during manufacturing rather than relying entirely on the chemistry of the original ingredients.

Lower Temperatures Prevent Damage to Glass

Another major advantage of the discovery is that it overcomes a longstanding problem in manufacturing specialized glasses.

Some of the materials investigated are unable to withstand the temperatures normally required to melt them. Instead of becoming usable glass, they begin to break down, damaging their structure and producing unwanted impurities.

The new molecular approach avoids much of this problem by allowing the materials to melt under gentler conditions.

"Thanks to this molecular trick, the material melts at significantly lower temperatures and remains stable. Studies on cobalt-containing glasses have shown that this gentler process prevents the formation of harmful decomposition products," explains Prof. Dr. Matthias Bauer from Paderborn University.

Preventing these unwanted byproducts is particularly important when studying magnetic properties. Impurities can interfere with measurements and conceal the material's actual magnetic behavior. By keeping the glass chemically stable, the researchers can observe these effects more clearly.

Advanced X-ray Measurements Confirm the Changes

To verify that the molecular treatment genuinely altered the glass, the research team turned to sophisticated analytical techniques.

Studying glass presents a challenge because its atoms do not follow the regular, repeating arrangement found in crystalline materials. This limits what conventional X-ray methods can reveal about its internal structure.

Prof. Bauer explains: "Instead, we used X-ray absorption spectroscopy, amongst other techniques. This method enabled us to investigate the immediate surroundings of the cobalt atoms."

The measurements provided strong evidence that the new molecule changes the arrangement of atoms around the metal centers.

Although the cobalt atoms maintained the same chemical state (oxidation state), their local surroundings changed considerably. The bonds connecting them to nearby molecules were reorganized to accommodate the added phenanthroline.

These observations confirmed that the method does more than simply help the material melt. It changes the underlying chemistry of the glass itself.

A New Generation of Glass With Tunable Properties

The researchers also demonstrated that their approach works beyond the original materials they investigated. Successful experiments with carboxylate-based framework structures suggest that the technique could be applied to a broader range of glass materials.

This versatility is especially promising because it transforms the melting stage of production into an opportunity to design new material properties.

Prof. Henke summarizes the significance for the future: "The melt is no longer a rigid intermediate state. It becomes a reaction space in which we can program the structure."

The ability to precisely modify metal centers could eventually lead to advanced glass components designed for specific technological purposes.

Potential applications include chemical catalysts, sensors, and optoelectronic devices that use interactions between light and electricity. Researchers could also develop materials capable of controlling magnetic behavior, manipulating light, or influencing chemical reactions with greater precision.

By turning molten glass into a material whose chemistry can be deliberately adjusted, the discovery offers a new route toward specialized glasses with properties that conventional manufacturing techniques could not easily produce.

#4409. 10 Best GameCube JRPGs That You Need to Play in Fall 2026

Contributor at DualShockers, former Esports Insider DACH content lead, former Escapist Magazine Germany content lead, software engineering background.

There’s always a specific moment every year where I realise that autumn has properly arrived. The evenings start drawing in before I’ve even had the chance to notice, the air gets crisper, and my coffee suddenly needs to be hot enough to warm both hands around the mug. I don’t think of myself as someone who hibernates, but I’d be lying if I said I didn’t naturally start staying in a little more this time of year.

And honestly? I love it. Being cozied up on my sofa with a blanket, a hot drink and the rain doing its thing outside is one of my favourite feelings, and it always seems to pull me towards games that tug on my nostalgia heartstrings. More often than not, that means the GameCube. Its JRPG library was smaller than what you’d find on its competitors, but it was stranger, braver and far more charming than it ever got credit for.

So many GameCube games have managed to escape the console in some way, but there are some JRPGs still waiting to abandon ship.

Some of these games have since found their way onto modern hardware, whilst others are still very much living in 2004, waiting for you to dig out an old memory card. A couple of them are certified classics, a few are delightfully weird, and at least one asks you to keep a close eye on the expiry date of your bananas. So grab a blanket, put the kettle on, and let’s take a look at the ten GameCube JRPGs that deserve a spot in your autumn rotation.

Tales of Symphonia was a big deal for GameCube owners. Released in Japan in August 2003, before reaching North America in July 2004 and Europe that November, it was the first Tales game to make the jump into 3D, complete with gorgeous cel-shaded visuals and character designs by Kosuke Fujishima. You follow Lloyd Irving and his childhood friend Colette, the Chosen One, on a journey to regenerate the dying world of Sylvarant. Naturally, things turn out to be a lot more complicated than that.

What made it really special, though, was the multiplayer. Up to four people could plug in a controller and take over a party member in the real-time battles, even if the camera stubbornly stuck to player one, leaving everyone else to fend for themselves off-screen. Add in the optional skits you could trigger with the Z button and a soundtrack by Motoi Sakuraba, and you have a game that will happily eat 80 hours of your autumn. If digging out the original hardware isn’t for you, the 2023 remaster on Switch, PS4 and Xbox One is the easier way in.

Taking a franchise famous for its tight, side-scrolling action and turning it into a turn-based RPG sounds like a recipe for disaster. Capcom did it anyway in 2004, and the result is a wonderfully fun little oddity that also found its way onto the PlayStation 2. Set in the 23rd century, X, Zero and newcomer Shadow are sent to Giga City to put an end to a Reploid rebellion led by Epsilon, with everything revolving around a powerful new substance called Force Metal.

Battles are snappy, and Hyper Modes, which let your characters transform mid-fight for a temporary power boost, keep things from ever getting stale. Axl joins the fold along the way, as does a slick bounty hunter called Spider, and the cast as a whole has a lot more personality than I expected going in. It received a fairly average critical response at the time, but it sold well, and I think it has aged far better than its reputation suggests.

Baten Kaitos was developed by Monolith Soft and tri-Crescendo, published by Namco, and released in Japan in December 2003, before making its way west across 2004 and 2005. Its world is made up of islands floating high in the sky, with the oceans below reduced to nothing more than legend. Fittingly, the name comes from the Arabic for “belly of the whale”, and it’s also the name of a star in the constellation Cetus. You don’t play as the protagonist, Kalas, but as a Guardian Spirit bonded to him, and he will very happily talk to you directly.

Everything revolves around Magnus, cards that capture the essence of objects, and with over 1,000 of them, deck building gets intricate fast. The fun part? Many Magnus change in real time. Grapes go rotten, then turn into wine, then vinegar, and a perfectly good banana will eventually turn on you if you leave it sitting in your deck. The 2023 HD Remaster on Switch bundles it with its prequel, Baten Kaitos Origins, which is a lovely excuse to finally experience both.

Path of Radiance launched in 2005 as the ninth main entry in the series, but only the third to make it to the West. It was the first Fire Emblem on a home console since Thracia 776, and it brought a few firsts along with it: 3D maps, voice acting and full motion cutscenes. You take control of Ike, a young mercenary who ends up at the centre of a war on the continent of Tellius, where the human beorc and the half-human laguz share a long, complicated history of mistrust.

Ike went on to become one of the series’ most beloved characters, joining the roster of Super Smash Bros. Brawl and later topping the men’s side of the very first Choose Your Legends poll in Fire Emblem Heroes. Permadeath is, of course, still very much a thing, so be prepared for heartbreak if you get careless. Players with save data from the Game Boy Advance Fire Emblem games could even link up to unlock concept art and special maps, which is the kind of connectivity I often find myself missing nowadays.

For years, a physical copy cost an arm and a leg. Thankfully, it joined the GameCube library on Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack in January 2026, so if you own a Switch 2, there has never been an easier time to sign up with the Greil Mercenaries. And should you get hooked, Radiant Dawn on the Wii picks up the story afterwards.

Skies of Arcadia first set sail on the Dreamcast in 2000, but for many of us, Legends on the GameCube was where we first met Vyse, Aika and Fina. You play as a Blue Rogue, essentially a sky pirate with a moral compass, in a world of floating continents orbited by six moons. The Valuan Empire is hunting down the Moon Crystals, and it falls to you and your crew to stop them, mostly by being extremely charming about it.

Exploration is at the heart of everything. Sailing into the unknown, stumbling across Discoveries and selling the information for a reward is ridiculously satisfying, and Legends bumped the total up to 89. The port also added Moonfish to hunt down and a bounty hunter named Piastol, whose side story finally explains how Vyse got that scar on his face. Crucially, it also toned down the random encounter rate, which anyone who survived the Dreamcast version will deeply appreciate.

If you're looking for some rough times on the Gamecube, here are 8 hard to beat Gamecube JRPGs.

Long before Demon’s Souls, FromSoftware made a card-based action RPG for the GameCube. Known as Rune in Japan, Lost Kingdoms released there in April 2002, with Activision publishing it in North America and Europe later that year. It was one of the very first JRPGs on the GameCube, and it shows in the best possible way: it’s a little rough, a little ambitious, and absolutely its own thing.

You play as Princess Katia, tasked with saving the five kingdoms of Argwyll from a mysterious fog that is swallowing the land. Instead of swinging a sword, you build a deck of cards, each one summoning a creature or weapon in real time, which makes every encounter feel like a frantic little puzzle. There’s even a two-player mode where you can pit your deck against a friend’s.

Reviews were average at the time, but it did well enough to get a sequel, Lost Kingdoms II, set 200 years later. Looking back now, it’s fascinating to see the studio already leaning into melancholy, fog-drenched fantasy a whole seven years before it would change everything. It’s not the most polished game on this list, but it might just be the most interesting.

The Thousand-Year Door released in 2004 and is still, for many, the high point of the Paper Mario series. After Princess Peach sends Mario a treasure map and promptly goes missing, he ends up in Rogueport, a rather grimy town sitting on top of a legendary door, and sets out to find the seven Crystal Stars. Along the way, you’ll pick up a wonderful cast of partners, from know-it-all Goombella to Admiral Bobbery, a retired sailor who just so happens to be a Bob-omb.

Battles take place on a literal stage in front of an audience, who can cheer you on, throw items at you or bring the set crashing down. Every chapter feels like a different genre, whether that’s climbing the ranks in the Glitz Pit wrestling arena or solving a whodunnit aboard the Excess Express. Meanwhile, Peach is on her own little adventure with a computer called TEC-XX, and the interludes where you take control of Bowser are pure comedic gold. If you’d rather not hunt down a GameCube copy, the 2024 Switch remake is a gorgeous way to play.

Pokémon Colosseum turned the formula on its head. There are no wild Pokémon to catch, no gyms to conquer, and instead of a wide-eyed kid, you play as Wes, a former member of Team Snagem who kicks off the game by blowing up their hideout. Set in the desert region of Orre, you use a Snag Machine to steal Shadow Pokémon, whose hearts have been closed off by Team Cipher, straight from other trainers.

Every battle is a double battle, you start with Espeon and Umbreon, and slowly purifying your Shadow Pokémon by fighting alongside them is a surprisingly heartfelt gameplay loop. In North America, pre-ordering the game got you a bonus disc that let you send a Jirachi to your copy of Ruby or Sapphire, which also fixed the infamous berry glitch. Europe, sadly, didn’t get one.

It sold 2.41 million copies worldwide, and its sequel, Pokémon XD: Gale of Darkness, joined the Switch 2’s GameCube library earlier this year. Colosseum was announced for the same service back in April 2025, and as of writing, we are still waiting for a release date. Patience is a virtue, or so they keep telling me.

Evolution Worlds is a curious one. Developed by Sting and published by Ubisoft outside of Japan, it arrived in 2002 as a compilation of two Dreamcast games, packing an abbreviated version of Evolution: The World of Sacred Device and the full Evolution 2: Far Off Promise onto one GameCube disc. Both games also received newly recorded English voice acting.

You play as Mag Launcher, a young adventurer exploring ancient ruins with a Cyframe, a powerful tool left behind by a long-lost civilisation. At its core, this is a turn-based dungeon crawler, and a genuinely charming one at that. It also has some of the most gloriously unhinged character names I’ve ever come across: Mag is joined by Linear Cannon, Chain Gun, Pepper Spray and his ever-loyal butler, Gre Nade.

I won’t pretend it’s the deepest game on this list. It really isn’t. But sometimes all you want on a rainy evening is a straightforward dungeon crawl with a lot of heart, and Evolution Worlds delivers exactly that. It’s comfort food in JRPG form, and there’s absolutely nothing wrong with that.

Final Fantasy Crystal Chronicles was a big moment, being the first Final Fantasy on a Nintendo home console since Final Fantasy VI back in 1994. Its world is covered in a poisonous miasma, and every village relies on a crystal to keep it at bay. Once a year, each village sends out a caravan to collect myrrh from distant trees, carrying a crystal chalice to protect them along the way, which many fans affectionately call the bucket.

The real hook was its multiplayer, and the price tag that came with it. Up to four players could join in, but every single one of them needed a Game Boy Advance and a link cable to act as their controller and personal screen. It was ambitious, a little bit impractical, and an absolute blast if you managed to pull it off. Playing solo, a Moogle carries the chalice for you instead.

You create your own caravanner from one of four tribes, the Clavat, Lilty, Yuke or Selkie, and set off into a world that rewards slow, patient journeys. If wrangling four GBAs sounds like a bit much, the 2020 Remastered Edition added online multiplayer, so your friends can join from the comfort of their own sofas. The myrrh only needs collecting once a year, after all.

Even though the GameCube didn't have a massive library, it did feature several fun and ambitious JRPG adventures.

#4408. Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 Review - Silver Bullet

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 arrives at a crossroads for the series, thanks in large part to the inconsistent quality of recent entries. With a shaky predecessor, Infinity Ward had a lot to repair and conclude, especially with 4 set to bookend the rebooted Modern Warfare series. Fortunately, backed up by a fun campaign, thrilling multiplayer, and loads of new modes and content, Modern Warfare 4 makes up for the past and then some.

Modern Warfare 4 continues after the events of 2023’s Modern Warfare 3, with Captain Price hellbent on stopping Makarov and his higher-ups. The story features shifting perspectives, from a new group of ragtag Korean soldiers to familiar characters like Gaz. The character dynamics harken back to the original trilogy, especially in the boots-on-the-ground missions with the South Korean unit, led by Park (played by Beef actor Young Mazino).

For a series that, at least recently, has been more spectacle than story, giving the stakes the time they deserve is nice. While it moves away from the stealthy and modernized elements, it makes sense for the matters at hand. The majority of Modern Warfare 4’s attempts at wrapping up the overarching plot of the rebooted series works, but it rushes through some character arcs and story beats in uneven fashion. Furthermore, much of the game’s cast, especially Mads Mikkelson’s Archer and Prisca Kim’s Ri Ju-Young, are underutilized, which is a shame since they both deliver great performances.

Despite the shortcomings of the campaign, Call of Duty's bread and butter, multiplayer, still delivers. While it doesn’t have the fluidity of Black Ops’ newer entries, the customization and design of weapons and maps make it worth digging into. From small, intimate shooting galleries with Mumbai and Nautical to wide free-for-alls like Coal and Reactor U92, the range helps maintain excitement, even if it gets repetitive over time.

The variety of multiplayer modes keeps things fresh on the battlefield. Returning modes like standard Team Deathmatch and Kill Confirmed continue that enjoyable competitive flair that made them the stars that they are. However, new modes like Combat Outpost and Hijack fit right into the already great lineup. In particular, Combat Outpost upscales your typical 6v6 player count to 24v24, leading to more action and teamwork. Hanging onto a team’s tank, shooting enemies from afar, and taking back outposts is exhilarating, even if it can all go bad moments later by a well-placed RPG shot.

Even after hours of gameplay, the variety of options to craft your perfect gun is impressive. Figuring out the best scope, ammo, stock, and muzzle, as well as the advantages and disadvantages of them, is a fun way of customizing your playstyle. Gunny, a mechanic that helps optimize your gun for certain styles, can help with decision paralysis, but I rarely used it. Not many FPSs go that far and Modern Warfare 4’s commitment to the feature makes it stand out.

The newest mode, DMZ, impresses out of the gate. After a few flat attempts in the past, this is the definitive Call of Duty extraction shooter, whether you play solo, or in duos or trios. Immediately, you’re thrust into the wide open world of Hajin and left to fend for yourselves with what you have and what you can gather and extract. Fans of Arc Raiders and Marathon should feel right at home as the gameplay borrows from the typical extraction shooter experience. Intense, action-packed moments keep you coming back after every win or loss. And the excellent gunplay and level design elevate it into something worthwhile, no matter how you play.

Despite not encountering many live players during my time in Hajin in DMZ, it still proves challenging, even for seasoned pros. The world is not your friend, and taking risks can come at a high cost. A good team, as well as a thoughtful loadout and traits, are required to survive. The unpredictability of it all keeps you on your toes, making for an exciting addition to the already strong multiplayer suite.

Regardless of the mode, Modern Warfare 4 is one of the best-looking Call of Duty titles to date. New York and Paris are lifelike, and it truly embodies the realistic, modern aesthetic the series has always aimed to achieve. However, I encountered a few technical hiccups, especially in the campaign. Slow framerate plagues some high-octane scenes and texture loading is frequent across the board. These distractions are far from game-breaking, but enough to be noticeable.

While the plot execution is a bit shaky, engaging multiplayer options, including DMZ, aptly demonstrate that Infinity Ward can still deliver compelling military-FPS experiences. Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 is a strong return to form that serves as a solid sendoff for the rebooted subseries.
